A thematic choropleth map series comparing effective labor market radii around major employment centers in Tokyo and Berlin, drawn from integrated transit timetables, census microdata, and establishment-level payroll records. The visualization employs a modified Hansen-type accessibility index calibrated to account for modal substitution effects and temporal congestion variation, with isochrone boundaries rendered at 30-minute, 60-minute, and 90-minute effective travel thresholds during morning peak periods. Tokyo data derive from the Person Trip Survey (2018) and Tokyo Metro OD matrices; Berlin sources include the Berlin-Brandenburg Verkehrsverbund (VBB) journey planner API sampled at 15-minute intervals across 2019–2021, merged with Bundesagentur für Arbeit establishment reports and the Mikrozensus scientific use files. The accompanying scatterplot matrices relate accessibility scores to sectoral wage premia and firm entry rates, with LOESS smoothing and 95% confidence intervals. All coordinate systems use WGS84 with Eckert IV projection for comparative panels; inset detail maps employ JGD2011 and ETRS89 respectively. Scale bars indicate approximate distortion; note that rail network density in the Tama subcenter zone versus Berlin's U-Bahn gaps in Treptow-Köpenick produces asymmetric contour geometries that resist direct scalar comparison without kernel normalization.

The spatial representation of labor market accessibility has become indispensable to understanding contemporary firm location decisions, yet comparative metropolitan analysis remains methodologically fraught. This visualization addresses the tension between transit infrastructure legacies and emerging flexible work arrangements, presenting integrated commute shed data for Tokyo's 23 special wards plus seven major suburban centers and Berlin's twelve Bezirke with disaggregated neighborhood-level resolution. The underlying premise, drawn from Anas, Arnott, and Small's foundational synthesis (1998) and more recent contributions by Ahlfeldt and Pierrostefani (2019), holds that effective labor pool size—rather than simple population density—determines agglomeration economies accessible to establishments. However, the operationalization of "effective" remains contested, particularly where transit systems exhibit high variance in temporal reliability.

Tokyo's rail-centric morphology generates distinctive accessibility topography. The Yamanote Loop and radial private railways produce star-shaped isochrones with pronounced elongation along corridor axes, evident in the 60-minute contour extending to Hachiōji, 37.9 kilometers west of Shinjuku, versus the compressed 28.4 kilometers reached southeast toward Kisarazu where bay crossing and mode interchange impose friction. The visualization renders this through cumulative opportunity surfaces rather than simple Euclidean buffers, with color ramp intervals at 0.5 standard deviations from the metropolitan mean accessibility score. Sectors cluster differentially: financial services establishments in Marunouchi and Nihonbashi demonstrate sensitivity to 90-minute shed population exceeding 15 million, while precision manufacturing in the Tama Technology Cluster appears responsive to narrower 45-minute thresholds for specialized technical occupations. The kernel density surfaces suggest possible threshold effects around the 60-minute boundary, though endogeneity concerns—transit investment responds to anticipated demand, complicating causal attribution—require instrumental variable approaches elaborated in the technical appendix.

Berlin presents a contrasting case of inherited infrastructure and political boundary effects. The S-Bahn ring, historically bisected and subsequently reintegrated, generates a more annular accessibility pattern, yet U-Bahn network gaps in the former eastern districts produce notable concavities in the 30-minute isochrone around Adlershof, a designated Wissenschafts- und Wirtschaftsstandort. The visualization captures this through discontinuous opportunity surfaces, with color breaks indicating accessibility deficits relative to synthetic control locations matched on pre-1945 industrial structure. Post-1990 firm entry data, mapped at 500-meter grid resolution, reveal clustering along the extended U5 line (opened 2020), though whether this represents infrastructure-induced location shifts or anticipatory developer behavior remains analytically unresolved. The scatterplot matrix indicates a weaker correlation between accessibility scores and service sector wage premia in Berlin (ρ = 0.34, p < 0.01) compared to Tokyo (ρ = 0.61, p < 0.001), potentially reflecting Berlin's historically compressed wage structure and smaller absolute labor market scale.

Methodological limitations warrant explicit acknowledgment. The Hansen index formulation, A_i = Σ_j P_j * f(t_ij), assumes exponential distance decay with parameters typically estimated from commuting flow data; here, the decay function is calibrated separately for each metropolitan area using revealed preference elasticities from workplace choice models. This preserves internal validity at potential cost to cross-sectional comparability, addressed through z-score normalization in the comparative panels. Temporal dynamics introduce additional complexity: Tokyo's "last train" phenomenon compresses effective evening accessibility, while Berlin's 24-hour weekend service expansion (partially suspended during 2020–2021) extends catchment for certain sectors. The visualization includes a toggle layer showing pandemic-period perturbations, with March 2021 isochrones indicating 12–18% contraction in effective 60-minute populations for both centers, though recovery trajectories diverged subsequently.

The management implications, though cautiously framed, merit consideration. Human resource practitioners in multinational firms have historically relied on crude radius-based recruitment assumptions; these representations suggest substantial optimization potential through granular accessibility assessment, particularly for skill-segmented positions where labor supply constraints bind. The Berlin-Brandenburg region's ongoing Verkehrsverbund tariff integration and Tokyo's anticipated Linear Chūō Shinkansen (opening 2027, with contested local employment effects) will require updated visualization as implementation proceeds. Replication materials, including Python scripts for isochrone generation and Stata do-files for establishment-level regression specifications, are deposited with the Harvard Dataverse under restricted-access protocols compliant with German and Japanese statistical confidentiality requirements.

body:
For eleven years, the wooden crate sat behind the coal chute in the presbytery cellar of St. Bartholomew's in Jelenia Góra, a Polish town of some seventy thousand souls tucked into the valley where the Bóbr River comes down out of the Karkonosze mountains. The crate was labeled, in a hand nobody now living could identify, with the single German word *Kirchenbücher* — church books. Everyone assumed it held parish registers, the endless columns of baptisms and burials that fill the archives of every European town and interest almost no one but genealogists and the occasional graduate student.

It was Father Marek Wilczyński who finally opened it, in October of the year the diocese ordered a survey of all parish holdings ahead of a long-deferred renovation. He was looking for a leak. What he found, wrapped in a sheet of newsprint from 1946 that carried an advertisement for bicycle tires, was not a register at all. It was a bound quire of roughly ninety leaves, hand-copied in a cramped Gothic cursive, and its first page bore a title in Latin and then, beneath it, a second title in a language that the priest recognized instantly and could not read: German, yes, but German shot through with something older and rougher, with spellings that swam and reeled.

"I knew it was theatre," Father Wilczyński says now, sitting in the parish office with the manuscript's digital facsimile open on a laptop before him. "There were speech prefixes. Names, then colons. *Iudas. Maria Magdalena. Longinus.* You don't need to be a philologist to see a play."

What he had found, as scholars from the University of Wrocław and the Herder Institute in Marburg would establish over the following two years, was a Passion play — a dramatization of Christ's suffering and death — copied in the last quarter of the sixteenth century from an exemplar that was very likely older still. It is not the earliest such text from the region. It is not the longest. But it may be the strangest, and for the town whose name it bears in its colophon, it has been something closer to a mirror suddenly uncovered.

The Passion play is one of the oldest continuous forms of European drama, and one of the most misunderstood. It is easy to imagine such works as pious, static, edifying — devotional tableaux with pauses for hymns. The reality of the medieval and early modern tradition is closer to something raucous, sprawling, and unnervingly modern. These plays ran for days. They employed hundreds. They combined liturgical solemnity with slapstick violence, theological exposition with obscene comedy. The soldiers who cast dice for Christ's garment made off-color jokes. Devils cavorted in the aisles and dragged sinners into hell-mouths built of painted canvas and smoke. In some towns the crucifixion was staged with such realism that municipal authorities issued ordinances limiting how long an actor could hang.

Silesia — the historically contested region that spreads across what is now southwestern Poland, with fingers reaching into the Czech Republic and eastern Germany — had a rich Passion tradition, and almost none of it survives. This is a matter of accident, of confession, and of catastrophe. The Reformation swept through the Silesian towns in the 1520s and 1530s with remarkable speed, and Lutheran magistrates had little patience for a genre they associated with what one Wrocław preacher called "the theatre of the Mass." Plays were suppressed, texts were repurposed as bindings and wrappers, and the great civic productions dwindled into village entertainments. Then came the Thirty Years' War, and after it the Prussian conquest of 1740, and after that the twentieth century, which in Silesia meant a near-total exchange of populations: the German inhabitants expelled westward after 1945, Poles from the eastern territories resettled in their place, and libraries, archives, and parish holdings scattered, burned, looted, or simply abandoned to rot.

That a Silesian Passion manuscript survived at all is unusual. That it survived in a town that after 1945 had no continuity of population, language, or religious practice with the community that produced it is, in the words of the Wrocław medievalist Dr. Hanna Zielińska, "close to a scandal of good luck."

Dr. Zielińska has spent much of the past three years with the text. She is fifty-four, speaks in long sentences that double back to correct themselves, and has the particular animation of a scholar who has stopped worrying whether her subject sounds important.

"The first thing you notice," she says, "is that it is not a play about Jesus. Not primarily. It is a play about Judas."

This is the source of the manuscript's growing reputation. Roughly a third of its surviving lines belong to Judas Iscariot, and they constitute what Dr. Zielińska calls "an argument, not a lament." The Judas of the medieval stage is typically a grotesque: greedy, cowardly, sometimes literally yellow-costumed, sometimes shown with a red wig and a moneybag, a figure whose damnation is never in doubt and whose function is to give the audience someone safe to hate. He despairs, he hangs himself, devils extract his soul through his ruptured belly in fulfillment of the description in Acts.

The Jelenia Góra Judas does all of these things. But between the betrayal and the suicide, the text gives him a monologue of two hundred and six lines in which he does something almost unheard of in the genre: he reasons.

The argument, as Dr. Zielińska reconstructs it, runs roughly thus. If the prophets foretold the betrayal, then the betrayal was necessary. If it was necessary, then someone had to perform it. If someone had to perform it, then that person was chosen — chosen as surely as Peter was chosen to deny and Mary was chosen to bear. And if he was chosen for a role in the economy of salvation, then how can the choosing itself be held against him? "*Ich bin der nagel in dem holcz*," the manuscript has him say — I am the nail in the wood — "*und ohn den nagel keyn crucz*." And without the nail, no cross.

"He is doing theology," Dr. Zielińska says. "Bad theology, from the standpoint of the sixteenth-century church, but real theology. He is putting his finger precisely on the problem of divine foreknowledge and human freedom, which is the problem, the problem Augustine and Boethius and Aquinas and Luther all break their teeth on. And he is putting it in the mouth of a stage villain, in the vernacular, in front of a market-square audience of butchers and weavers and children."

The manuscript does not let Judas win. A figure identified only as *Vox de Nube* — the Voice from the Cloud — answers him in seventy-odd lines, and the answer is orthodox: that foreknowledge is not compulsion, that God's seeing is not God's forcing, that Judas was offered the same grace as Peter and chose otherwise, and that his sin lies not in the betrayal but in the despair that followed it. Peter also betrayed and was forgiven, because Peter wept and returned. Judas wept and did not return. The distinction the play draws is between two kinds of remorse — one that opens toward mercy, one that closes in on itself and becomes its own hell.

But here is the thing that has made the text interesting to people well beyond the small world of Silesian philology. The Voice from the Cloud gets seventy lines. Judas gets two hundred and six. And Judas gets the better poetry.

"That imbalance is not an accident of transmission," says Professor Andrzej Kubik of the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, who has written on the text's prosody. "The Judas monologue is metrically the most sophisticated passage in the manuscript. It uses a four-stress line with a shifting caesura, and there are internal rhymes that a copyist would not invent. Somebody worked on this. Somebody cared about making the wrong answer beautiful."

Why would they? The scholarly answers divide roughly into three camps, and the disagreement has been unusually public for a field where controversies normally play out over decades in the footnotes of Festschriften.

The first position, associated with Dr. Zielińska, holds that the play is a piece of pastoral engineering. Its purpose is not to present a fair debate but to inoculate. The town's preacher — and Dr. Zielińska thinks the author was a preacher, given the sermon-like structure of the Voice's reply — knew perfectly well that ordinary people harbored exactly Judas's doubts. Predestination was in the air; the fifteen-thirties and forties in Silesia were saturated with argument about grace and works and whether the damned had ever had a chance. Better, on this reading, to let the doubt be spoken aloud, in its strongest form, by a figure the audience already knows is wrong, and then to answer it. "You give the poison a face," she says, "so that the antidote has something to work on."

The second position, argued most forcefully by the German scholar Dr. Bernhard Hesse of Marburg, is that the play is quietly subversive — that its author was closer to sympathy with Judas than a Lutheran or Catholic town council would have tolerated, and that the orthodox reply is a fig leaf. Dr. Hesse points to a passage, badly damaged, in which the crowd at the crucifixion appears to speak lines that echo the Judas monologue, as though his argument had spread. He points also to the play's treatment of Pilate, who is granted an unusual measure of dignity, and to the total absence of the anti-Jewish invective that disfigures nearly every comparable text from the period.

That last point is not a small one, and it is worth dwelling on. The Passion play tradition is, historically, one of the great engines of European antisemitism. The genre's standard structure — in which a crowd of Jewish figures demands Christ's death and mocks his suffering — was performed annually, in town after town, for centuries, and it left marks that historians can trace in the pattern of pogroms. Many surviving texts include material of extraordinary viciousness. The Jelenia Góra manuscript does not. Its accusers are the Temple authorities, named and individualized; its crowd is fickle rather than malevolent; and there is no scene of collective mockery at the cross.

"I do not want to make this manuscript into something it is not," Dr. Hesse says carefully, by telephone from Marburg. "It is a Christian devotional text of the sixteenth century, and it takes for granted the theological supersessionism of its age. But somebody, at some point in its transmission, either omitted or refused to copy material that we find in virtually every parallel version. That is a choice. We cannot know whose choice, or why. But it is a choice, and I find it moving."

The third position, which has fewer adherents but a certain stubborn appeal, is that the play is simply a good play, and that its author was a dramatist first and a theologian second. On this view, Judas gets the best lines for the same reason Milton's Satan does, or Marlowe's Faustus: because a dramatist who is any good cannot help making a compelling case for the character whose interior he has to inhabit. Professor Kubik leans this way. "We keep asking what the author believed," he says. "Maybe the author believed in the theatre. Maybe he had a good actor for Judas and wrote to his strength. This is what happens in playhouses. It has always happened in playhouses."

Whatever its author intended, the manuscript has had an afterlife in Jelenia Góra that nobody anticipated.

The town, called Hirschberg im Riesengebirge until 1945, has had a difficult relationship with its own past. Its architecture is German — the arcaded houses around the market square, the Baroque churches, the villas along the river built by linen merchants who grew rich exporting Silesian cloth to Hamburg and Amsterdam. Its people are, overwhelmingly, the descendants of Poles resettled from Lwów and Volhynia and the Vilnius region, themselves expelled when the eastern border moved west. For decades the official position under state socialism was that Silesia had always been essentially Polish, briefly Germanized, now restored — a claim that required a certain amount of not looking at the buildings one lived in. The German dead in the cemeteries were an embarrassment; the German inscriptions on the churches were plastered over or ignored.

That has changed, unevenly and sometimes painfully, since 1989. There are now bilingual plaques. There is a foundation that maintains the old Protestant cemetery. There are annual meetings between the town and the association of expelled Hirschbergers and their children, meetings that began in mutual awkwardness and have become, participants say, something like friendship.

The Passion manuscript arrived in the middle of that slow negotiation, and it arrived without a clear owner.

"This is the part that people outside don't understand," says Katarzyna Nowak, who directs the regional museum housed in the former Protestant school. "A German text, copied by German hands, found in a Polish parish, in a Polish town, in a building that was Catholic before the Reformation and Protestant after it and Catholic again after 1945. Who does it belong to? Everybody has an argument. And for once, all the arguments are good."

The practical resolution has been a joint project: digitization by the university in Wrocław, conservation funded partly by the German federal cultural office for the historic eastern regions, a critical edition in preparation with editors from both countries, and — the part that has captured the town — a performance.

In the spring, on a temporary stage erected in the market square, a company of local amateurs performed a Polish translation of the Judas monologue and the Voice's reply, roughly forty minutes of the manuscript, before an audience the organizers estimate at eighteen hundred people. The translation was made by a retired schoolteacher from Cieplice, working from Dr. Zielińska's transcription with the help of her German-speaking granddaughter. The Judas was a forty-one-year-old refrigeration technician named Piotr Malec, who had last been on a stage in secondary school.

"I didn't understand it at first," Mr. Malec says. He is a big man with careful hands, and he says this without embarrassment. "I read it three times and I thought, this man is making excuses. That's all. He's a coward looking for a reason. And then the fourth time I read it I thought, no. He's right. That's the terrible thing. Everything he says is right, and he's still damned, and he knows he's still damned, and he says it anyway because he wants somebody to hear him."

He pauses.

"My grandmother came here from a village near Tarnopol. She never once said she was happy to be here. Never once. And she also never said she was unhappy. She just lived here for fifty years in somebody else's house and didn't complain and didn't pretend. When I was learning those lines, I kept hearing her. I don't know why. There's no connection."

There is, of course, and the town has felt it. What the audience in the market square heard, in a Polish translation of an anonymous German text about a Jewish disciple in Roman Judaea, was a man arguing that he had been placed in an intolerable position by forces he did not choose and could not resist, that he had done what the position required, and that he was going to be blamed for it forever.

"You cannot stage that here and expect it to stay in the first century," Ms. Nowak says drily.

Not everyone has welcomed the attention. Some in the parish were uneasy about a Judas granted so much sympathy; there were letters, and a homily on the subject that Father Wilczyński describes as "not my finest." A local councilman objected to German funding for the conservation on principle, and was voted down. A visiting journalist from Warsaw wrote a piece suggesting that the whole enterprise was an exercise in fashionable German-Polish reconciliation and that the manuscript was, philologically speaking, "a modest text inflated by politics."

Dr. Zielińska takes this last charge seriously, which is to her credit.

"He is not entirely wrong," she says. "It is a provincial manuscript. It is not the Frankfurt Passion play, it is not Alsfeld, it is not one of the great civic cycles. If you came to it looking only for literary monuments you would file it and move on. But that is a bad way to read the past. Most of the past was provincial. Most of what people actually saw and heard and argued about was made by people whose names we don't have, for audiences of a few hundred, in towns you have to look up. The great monuments survive because they were great, yes, but also because they were lucky, and because someone rich wanted them kept. This thing survived because a coal chute leaked slowly."

She turns the laptop toward the window to cut the glare, and scrolls to a leaf near the end, where the hand changes and the ink goes brown.

Here, in a different and later cursive, someone has written five lines in the bottom margin. They are not part of the play. Dr. Zielińska reads them aloud in the original and then translates.

"*I have copied this out for the third time and my eyes are failing. If a man reads this after me let him say a prayer for Christoph Neander, schoolmaster, who did not believe the arguments of Judas but could not answer them, and who hopes to be corrected in heaven.*"

The date, if it is a date, is smudged. The name Christoph Neander does not appear in the surviving Hirschberg town records, which are themselves fragmentary, having been transferred to Wrocław in 1942 and partly destroyed in 1945. There is a Neander recorded as a teacher in the nearby town of Kamienna Góra in the 1590s, but the identification is speculative and Dr. Zielińska refuses to make it.

"I would like him to be that man," she says. "I have no right to make him that man."

What is certain is that someone sat with this text long enough to copy it three times, and that the copying cost him his sight, and that he was honest enough to admit in the margin that he had lost the argument.

The critical edition is expected in eighteen months. The manuscript itself now lives in a climate-controlled case at the university library in Wrocław, on loan from the parish, which retains ownership. A facsimile is displayed in the museum in Jelenia Góra, open to the first leaf of the Judas monologue, with the Polish translation on a panel beside it and the German on the other side.

The company that performed in the market square has asked for permission to stage a longer version next year — perhaps ninety minutes, including the trial before Pilate and the fragmentary crowd scene that Dr. Hesse finds so provocative. Mr. Malec has agreed to return, on the condition that somebody else learn the lines as understudy. "Two hundred and six lines," he says. "In my job I remember serial numbers. This is different. This gets in."

Father Wilczyński, for his part, has resumed the survey of the parish holdings, which he abandoned in the excitement. He has been through the sacristy, the choir loft, and a walled-up niche behind the organ. So far he has found a nineteenth-century chalice, four hundred moldering hymnals, and a mouse nest constructed entirely from the shredded minutes of a 1908 building committee.

"People ask if I expect to find another one," he says. "I don't. But I didn't expect the first one. That's rather the point of the whole thing, isn't it. You go down looking for a leak."

WHEREAS, the State of São Paulo, acting through its competent environmental, scientific, and educational authorities, and the Commonwealth of Australia, acting through its competent scientific, environmental, and meteorological authorities, recognize that the Earth is a single physical system whose rocks, waters, atmosphere, and living communities are joined by processes that disregard political boundaries;

WHEREAS, the Parties acknowledge that the basalt terraces and red soils of the São Paulo interior, the Atlantic Forest and mangrove margins of the State’s coast, the ancient mineral landscapes of Western Australia, the Great Dividing Range, the Murray–Darling Basin, and the reefs, forests, deserts, and wetlands of the Australian continent constitute distinct archives of planetary history;

WHEREAS, the Parties further acknowledge that biological diversity is not an ornament placed upon the land, but an active inheritance shaped by geology, climate, fire, water, evolution, and the movement of species through time;

WHEREAS, changes in temperature, precipitation, ocean chemistry, sea level, wildfire regimes, and the frequency of extreme events may alter both natural systems and the communities that depend upon them;

WHEREAS, the Parties desire to promote the lawful exchange of observations, methods, samples, educational materials, and scientific expertise, while respecting sovereignty, Indigenous rights and knowledge, ethical requirements, access and benefit-sharing obligations, and the integrity of protected areas;

NOW, THEREFORE, the Parties record their common understanding as follows:

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

1. This Memorandum establishes a framework for cooperation concerning:

(a) the geological history and present condition of landscapes in São Paulo and Australia;

(b) biological diversity, ecological resilience, species distribution, and the conservation of habitats;

(c) climate observations, climate variability, climate change, and the effects thereof upon geological and biological systems;

(d) public education concerning the relation between rocks, living organisms, atmosphere, oceans, and human settlement; and

(e) the development of scientific practices capable of comparing observations made in tropical, subtropical, temperate, arid, coastal, and marine environments.

2. The cooperation contemplated herein may include joint research, reciprocal visits, technical workshops, public exhibitions, school programs, shared databases, field courses, remote sensing, laboratory analysis, and the preparation of reports for governmental and community use.

3. Nothing in this Memorandum shall be construed as creating a legal partnership, corporation, agency, or employment relationship between the Parties, nor shall it authorize either Party to bind the other, incur liability on behalf of the other, or represent that it possesses authority not expressly granted by its own laws.

II. SCIENTIFIC BASIS

4. The Parties recognize geology as the study of the Earth’s materials, structure, history, and processes. For purposes of the cooperation, geological observations may include, without limitation, the description of rocks and minerals, stratigraphic succession, soil formation, erosion, sediment transport, volcanic history, tectonic structure, groundwater movement, coastline change, and the alteration of landscapes by human activity.

5. The Parties recognize that the geological record is incomplete but indispensable. A granite outcrop, a volcanic plateau, a fossil-bearing layer, a coastal dune, or a river terrace may preserve evidence of events extending across intervals vastly longer than any human institution. Such evidence shall be treated not as inert scenery, but as a record from which changing environments may be inferred.

6. The State of São Paulo contains geological settings of particular relevance to comparative study, including the Paraná Basin, basaltic formations associated with the Serra Geral event, deeply weathered tropical soils, river systems draining toward the Paraná and Atlantic basins, coastal sedimentary environments, and landscapes in which urban expansion, agriculture, infrastructure, and forest remnants meet upon the same ground.

7. Australia contains geological settings of particular relevance to comparative study, including ancient cratonic provinces, the Great Artesian Basin, the Great Dividing Range, arid and semi-arid regolith, carbonate platforms, volcanic provinces, coastal sedimentary systems, and landscapes in which drought, fire, mining, pastoral use, urban development, and conservation occur in close relation.

8. The Parties recognize biology as the study of living systems, including organisms, populations, communities, ecosystems, heredity, adaptation, and the relations by which energy and matter pass through the living world.

9. The Parties shall give particular attention to the manner in which biological communities are conditioned by substrate, elevation, hydrology, temperature, disturbance, and geographic isolation. The Atlantic Forest, cerrado, wetlands, estuaries, and coastal ecosystems of São Paulo may therefore be compared, not as replicas, with Australian rainforests, savannas, woodlands, wetlands, deserts, mangroves, and reefs.

10. The Parties recognize that climate consists not merely of daily weather, but of the statistical character of atmospheric conditions over time, including temperature, precipitation, wind, humidity, radiation, drought, and the occurrence of extremes. Climate shall be examined together with ocean conditions, cryospheric processes where relevant, land cover, and the circulation of carbon and water through the Earth system.

11. The Parties further recognize that climate change may operate through gradual trends and abrupt events alike. A slow rise in mean temperature, a shift in the seasonal onset of rain, a longer interval between fires, a marine heatwave, a severe flood, or the failure of a pollinating species may each produce consequences that accumulate across generations.

III. GOVERNING PRINCIPLES

12. Cooperation under this Memorandum shall be guided by the following principles:

(a) scientific integrity, including transparent methods, preservation of data provenance, acknowledgment of uncertainty, and correction of material error;

(b) precaution, where an activity may cause serious or irreversible harm notwithstanding incomplete scientific knowledge;

(c) intergenerational responsibility, recognizing that present decisions may determine the conditions under which future communities live;

(d) respect for Indigenous peoples, their laws, cultural authority, knowledge systems, sacred places, and rights to determine whether and how knowledge is shared;

(e) conservation of biological diversity and the maintenance of ecological processes;

(f) equitable access to publicly funded results, subject to legitimate restrictions concerning privacy, cultural knowledge, security, endangered species, and intellectual property;

(g) proportionality, so that field activities and sampling do not cause harm greater than the knowledge reasonably expected to result; and

(h) recognition that local observations, including those maintained by farmers, fishers, Traditional Owners, Indigenous peoples, park rangers, and community organizations, may provide essential evidence when interpreted with appropriate care.

13. The Parties shall avoid presenting scientific projections as certainties where the evidence supports only a range of outcomes. Reports prepared under this Memorandum shall distinguish observed facts, analytical inferences, model projections, assumptions, and unresolved questions.

IV. JOINT PROGRAMS

14. The Parties may establish joint programs in the following areas.

15. GEOLOGICAL OBSERVATION AND LANDSCAPE CHANGE. The Parties may compare methods for mapping rock units, soils, erosion features, landslides, river sediments, dunes, coastal retreat, and groundwater-dependent formations. The work may include the use of satellite imagery, aerial photography, geographic information systems, geological maps, sediment cores, radiometric dating, geochemical analysis, and field photography taken from fixed observation points.

16. Where geological samples are collected, the collecting institution shall record the locality, date, depth or elevation, material description, purpose of collection, collector, and applicable permit. Samples shall not be removed from Indigenous land, protected land, marine territory, or any other regulated area without prior authorization.

17. BIOLOGICAL INVENTORY AND HABITAT CONDITION. The Parties may undertake surveys of plants, fungi, animals, microorganisms, and ecological communities, including work on pollinators, migratory species, freshwater organisms, reef-associated life, forest fragments, grasslands, wetlands, and species adapted to fire or drought.

18. Biological observations shall, where practicable, include the location, date, observer, method, abundance or frequency, habitat description, and confidence of identification. Records concerning threatened species or vulnerable nesting sites may be generalized, withheld, or subject to controlled access where disclosure would increase the risk of collection, disturbance, trafficking, or other harm.

19. The Parties shall encourage the use of non-destructive methods. Capture, marking, tissue sampling, removal of plants, disturbance of nests, handling of vertebrates, and collection of microorganisms shall be undertaken only by qualified persons and pursuant to applicable ethical review, permits, quarantine rules, and animal-welfare requirements.

20. CLIMATE AND EARTH-SYSTEM OBSERVATIONS. The Parties may exchange observations concerning air temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, solar radiation, soil moisture, streamflow, groundwater level, sea-surface temperature, ocean acidity, vegetation condition, fire scars, and other indicators of environmental change.

21. The Parties may compare historical records with instrumental observations, paleoclimate evidence, ecological surveys, and climate models. Such comparisons may assist in explaining why a landscape appears resilient to one disturbance yet vulnerable to another, or why a species may persist in one locality while disappearing from a neighboring one.

22. The Parties may cooperate in preparing plain-language climate information for municipalities, schools, protected-area managers, farmers, and coastal communities. Such information shall state the period considered, the geographical scale, the principal assumptions, and the limits of the available evidence.

V. INSTITUTIONAL ARRANGEMENTS

23. Each Party shall designate a focal institution for ordinary coordination. The designated institution for the State of São Paulo may include the Instituto Geológico, the Instituto Florestal, the Instituto de Botânica, the Fundação Florestal, universities established or maintained in the State, or another competent public body. The designated institution for Australia may include Geoscience Australia, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, the Australian Bureau of Meteorology, Parks Australia, a state or territory authority, or another competent public body.

24. The focal institutions may constitute a Joint Scientific Committee consisting of an equal number of representatives appointed by the Parties. The Committee may invite universities, museums, observatories, Indigenous representatives, community organizations, and technical experts to participate according to the subject under consideration.

25. The Committee shall meet at least once in each calendar year, in person or by electronic means, and shall:

(a) identify priorities for joint work;

(b) review proposed field activities and data exchanges;

(c) recommend standards for recording, archiving, and publishing observations;

(d) identify funding opportunities;

(e) evaluate educational and public-engagement activities; and

(f) prepare a summary of achievements, difficulties, and proposed future work.

26. No recommendation of the Committee shall authorize a field activity, expenditure, export, import, publication, or disclosure that is prohibited by the law of either Party.

VI. DATA, SAMPLES, AND PUBLICATION

27. Each Party shall endeavor to make non-sensitive data generated through joint activities available to the scientific community and the public within a reasonable period after quality assurance.

28. Data shall be accompanied, where practicable, by descriptions of collection methods, instruments, calibration, spatial and temporal coverage, processing steps, uncertainty, and known limitations. A number without its history may appear precise while remaining scientifically weak; the Parties therefore agree that context is part of the record.

29. The Parties shall consult before releasing information that may:

(a) identify a sacred or culturally restricted place;

(b) reveal the location of a threatened species or vulnerable archaeological site;

(c) contain personal information;

(d) breach a permit, quarantine requirement, access agreement, or confidentiality obligation; or

(e) compromise national security, public safety, or the lawful interests of an Indigenous community.

30. Samples transferred between the Parties shall be accompanied by written records specifying ownership or custody, permitted uses, storage conditions, hazardous properties, biosecurity requirements, and the disposition of remaining material. No recipient shall transfer a sample to a third party without the written consent of the originating institution and any consent required by law.

31. The Parties shall seek to publish joint results in a manner that gives appropriate credit to field workers, laboratory staff, data custodians, Indigenous knowledge holders, students, and collaborating institutions. Authorship shall reflect substantial intellectual or practical contribution and shall not be assigned solely by rank or office.

32. Prior to publication, each Party may review a proposed manuscript solely to identify confidential information, security concerns, errors concerning its institutions or territory, or obligations imposed by law. Such review shall not be used to suppress a scientifically supported conclusion merely because it is inconvenient or unfavorable.

VII. INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE AND CULTURAL AUTHORITY

33. The Parties acknowledge that knowledge of land, water, seasons, species behavior, fire, stars, winds, and ecological change may be held within Indigenous communities through laws and practices that are not reducible to a dataset.

34. No Indigenous knowledge shall be recorded, translated, published, commercialized, or incorporated into a scientific product without the free, prior, and informed consent of the relevant knowledge holders and without agreement concerning attribution, access, control, benefit sharing, and future use.

35. In São Paulo, activities shall respect the rights and authorities of Indigenous peoples and traditional communities, including communities whose territories, cultural sites, or customary practices may be affected by research. In Australia, activities shall respect the rights and authorities of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, including Traditional Owners and their representative bodies.

36. Where scientific and Indigenous knowledge are brought into dialogue, neither shall be presented as a decorative supplement to the other. The Parties shall state the source, scope, and appropriate interpretation of each body of knowledge, recognizing that different methods may answer different questions and may carry different obligations.

VIII. FIELD SAFETY AND ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION

37. Each field activity shall be preceded by an assessment of safety, access, weather, terrain, fire, flood, wildlife, disease, communications, transport, and emergency response. Activities in the cerrado, Atlantic Forest, Australian bush, desert, reef, wetland, or remote inland region shall account for local hazards rather than relying upon general assumptions.

38. Participants shall comply with instructions issued by landholders, park authorities, Indigenous authorities, emergency services, and biosecurity officials. The presence of a permit shall not excuse conduct that damages a site, disturbs wildlife, spreads disease, introduces organisms, or places persons at unreasonable risk.

39. Field teams shall remove equipment, waste, temporary markers, and non-native material unless an authority directs otherwise. Vehicles and footwear shall be cleaned where required to prevent the movement of seeds, fungi, pathogens, or soil organisms between ecosystems.

40. Fire-related research shall be conducted with particular care. The Parties recognize that fire may be an ecological process, a cultural practice, a hazard, and a source of atmospheric emissions, depending upon place, season, intensity, and management. No experimental burn shall occur without all required approvals and a plan for containment, monitoring, and cessation.

IX. EDUCATION AND PUBLIC COMMUNICATION

41. The Parties may develop exhibits, maps, classroom materials, public lectures, documentary programs, and traveling displays showing how a stone, a seed, a river, a cloud, and a city may be understood as participants in one changing system.

42. Materials prepared for non-specialists shall avoid unnecessary technical language while preserving scientific meaning. Terms such as “weather,” “climate,” “habitat,” “species,” “carbon cycle,” “erosion,” and “biodiversity” shall be explained through examples drawn from recognizable places, including the Tietê and Paraná river systems, the Serra do Mar, the coastal zone of São Paulo, the Murray–Darling Basin, the Great Barrier Reef, the Australian Alps, and the arid interior.

43. Educational materials shall make clear that uncertainty is not ignorance. A forecast may carry uncertainty because the atmosphere is complex, observations are incomplete, or several future pathways remain possible. Stating that uncertainty honestly permits communities to prepare for risk without mistaking a range of outcomes for a promise.

44. The Parties shall encourage students to distinguish observation from explanation. A dark band in a rock, a decline in frog calls, a date of flowering, or a measured rise in water temperature is an observation. The account of what caused it is an interpretation requiring evidence, comparison, and, where possible, independent testing.

X. FUNDING AND INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY

45. Activities under this Memorandum shall be subject to the availability of funds and personnel. Each Party shall ordinarily bear its own expenses unless a separate written arrangement provides otherwise.

46. A Party receiving external funding for a joint activity shall inform the other Party of material conditions attached to that funding. No funding condition shall be accepted if it requires the concealment, falsification, or unreasonable restriction of scientific results.

47. Intellectual property created jointly shall be governed by a written arrangement adopted before substantial work begins. That arrangement shall address ownership, licensing, commercial use, attribution, protection of confidential information, and the rights of students and early-career researchers.

48. Pre-existing materials shall remain the property of the Party or institution that supplied them, unless otherwise agreed. A license to use such materials shall be limited to the purpose for which it is granted and shall not be presumed to include commercial exploitation.

XI. LIABILITY, DISPUTES, AND AMENDMENT

49. Each Party shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of its personnel in accordance with applicable law. Neither Party shall be liable for indirect or consequential loss arising solely from the voluntary exchange of information, except to the extent liability cannot lawfully be excluded.

50. Any disagreement concerning the interpretation or implementation of this Memorandum shall first be referred to the focal institutions. If unresolved, it shall be submitted to the Joint Scientific Committee and thereafter to the competent authorities designated by the Parties.

51. This Memorandum may be amended by written agreement of the Parties. An amendment shall enter into effect on the date specified therein or, if no date is specified, upon signature by the authorized representatives.

52. Either Party may terminate this Memorandum by written notice to the other Party. Termination shall not affect activities already commenced, obligations concerning confidentiality, sample custody, Indigenous consent, publication, data protection, or the safe return or disposal of materials, unless the Parties agree otherwise.

XII. FINAL PROVISIONS

53. This Memorandum is intended to express cooperation and mutual understanding and does not, by itself, create rights or obligations enforceable under international or domestic law. Any activity requiring a binding commitment shall be governed by a separate instrument executed by authorized representatives.

54. Nothing herein shall limit the power of either Party to protect public health, human safety, cultural heritage, endangered species, national security, or the integrity of scientific and environmental records.

55. The Parties affirm that the purposes of this Memorandum are best served by patience in observation, rigor in analysis, humility before complexity, and care for places that cannot speak in legal proceedings yet bear the consequences of every decision made about them.

56. The authorized representatives of the State of São Paulo and the Commonwealth of Australia, acting in accordance with their respective procedures, may sign this Memorandum in duplicate originals, each text being equally valid, on the dates appearing beneath their signatures.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the undersigned have executed this Memorandum.

FOR THE STATE OF SÃO PAULO

Name: ______________________________

Title: _______________________________

Date: _______________________________

Signature: ___________________________

FOR THE COMMONWEALTH OF AUSTRALIA

Monday, 8 April

I spent the morning comparing Brazil’s coastal defense with Russia’s continental tradition. Brazil’s forts at Salvador and along the Amazon guarded ports, rivers, and trade routes; geography made mobility and supply as important as artillery. Russia faced wider land frontiers, so defense grew around depth, fortifications, and mass armies. From the Romanov period through the Soviet Union, commanders repeatedly traded space for time—most dramatically against Napoleon in 1812 and Germany in 1941.

Tuesday, 9 April

The contrast remains striking today. Brazil’s defense planning still emphasizes the Atlantic, the Amazon, border surveillance, and peacekeeping experience, while Russia maintains a nuclear deterrent, layered air defenses, and major land forces. Neither story is purely military: roads, shipyards, industry, diplomacy, and public support matter just as much. History makes the point clearly—defense is shaped less by abstract doctrine than by territory, neighbors, and the resources a state can sustain.

Gather round the market square,
where fisherfolk and traders share.
The net pulls heavy, silver-bright,
beneath the warm Caribbean light.

But see the coral, pale and thin,
where commerce ends and care begins.
We guard the reef, our common wealth,
to keep the ecosystem's health.

No child goes hungry, no wave turns sour,
if we protect this island bower.
So sing the song of give and take,
for ocean's sake and neighbor's sake.

Along North Carolina’s coast, the Coast Guard operates where public safety and national power meet. From stations at Oregon Inlet, Fort Macon, and Wrightsville Beach, crews patrol waters used by fishermen, commercial ships, recreational boaters, and offshore energy interests. Their work is practical—rescuing mariners, enforcing navigation rules, and protecting ports—but it also reflects the character of government.

A democratic government exercises authority through established law, public oversight, and clearly defined missions. Coast Guard personnel may board a vessel, close an unsafe channel, or direct traffic during a storm, yet those actions are limited by statute and accountable to civilian leadership. The authority is strong because it is predictable.

Authoritarian governments often present maritime security differently. They may place naval forces under direct political control, use port access and shipping regulations to pressure neighboring states, or treat coast guard patrols as instruments of intimidation. The distinction is not simply between military and civilian vessels. It lies in whether maritime power serves public rules or the unchecked preferences of those in command.

For North Carolina communities, this distinction matters beyond the horizon. Secure sea lanes, lawful commerce, and reliable rescue services depend on institutions that are capable, disciplined, and answerable to the public.

Host:
Good afternoon, and welcome to Cross-Border History. I am Elena Vasquez, joining you from Toronto. Today we examine the development of democracy from ancient origins through wars and the formation of modern nations, with particular attention to Canada and the United States. Our guest is Dr. James Harrington, professor of political history at Georgetown University in Washington.

Dr. Harrington:
Thank you, Elena. It is a pleasure to join you.

Host:
How did ancient civilizations first shape the idea of democracy?

Dr. Harrington:
The clearest early example is fifth-century Athens, where eligible male citizens voted directly in the assembly. Participation was narrow, excluding women, slaves, and non-citizens, yet it established the principle that political power could rest with the people rather than a monarch. The Roman Republic added representative mechanisms through the Senate and elected consuls, ideas that later Enlightenment writers would adapt.

Host:
How did those ideas reach North America, especially through conflict?

Dr. Harrington:
Enlightenment thinkers revived classical models. In the United States the Revolutionary War of 1775-1783 was framed as resistance to tyranny and produced the 1787 Constitution, with its separation of powers drawn from mixed-government theory. Canada followed a different path inside the British parliamentary tradition. The War of 1812 tested allegiances but did not produce a comparable break. Confederation in 1867 created a federal system based on responsible government, without a revolutionary founding war.

Host:
What role have later wars played in both countries?

Dr. Harrington:
The world wars of the twentieth century strengthened democratic self-understanding by contrasting it with authoritarianism. Suffrage expanded in both nations around the First World War. The Second World War and the subsequent Cold War further identified democracy with individual rights and representative institutions. Canada’s parliamentary system and the United States’ presidential system continue to reflect those distinct historical origins while facing similar contemporary pressures.

Host:
Thank you, Dr. Harrington. That concludes this episode.

body:
Suryadi Hartono, whose paintings and sculptures reshaped the dialogue between phenomenological philosophy and visual practice across Southeast Asia and Australia, died on 11 February 2023 in Yogyakarta. He was 84. His death was confirmed by the Singapore Art Museum, which had maintained a long curatorial relationship with the artist since his first major retrospective there in 2001. Hartono's work, spanning six decades, is held in the permanent collections of the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra, the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne, the Art Gallery of New South Wales in Sydney, the Singapore Art Museum, and the Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art in Nusantara.

Born in Surakarta, Central Java, on 3 May 1938, Hartono came of age during the Indonesian National Revolution and the subsequent political consolidations of the 1950s. He enrolled at the Indonesian Academy of Fine Arts, ASRI, in Yogyakarta in 1957, studying under Sudjojono and Affandi, but his education was interrupted by the political upheavals of the mid-1960s. He completed his diploma in 1968, by which time his drawing had already moved away from the socially committed realism favoured by his teachers toward a more introspective investigation of perception itself.

In 1971 Hartono received a Colombo Plan scholarship to study at the Victorian College of the Arts in Melbourne. The decision to relocate to Australia was, by his own account, driven less by aesthetic considerations than by the opportunity to read Maurice Merleau-Ponty and Edmund Husserl in a library that held them. His three years in Melbourne proved decisive. He encountered the work of the Australian tonalist painters William Beckwith McInnes and Clarice Beckett, whose approaches to atmospheric light he studied closely, and he began a correspondence with the Melbourne-based philosopher Vincent Buckley, then a professor at the University of Melbourne, whose writings on presence and embodied cognition would inform Hartono's practice for the remainder of his life.

Hartono returned to Yogyakarta in 1974 and established a studio in the Bantul district, where he would work for the next five decades. The paintings of the late 1970s, many of them small-scale oils on board, mark the emergence of his mature idiom. These works, such as "Lapisan Pertama" (First Layer, 1976) and "Ruang Diam" (Quiet Space, 1978), deploy a restricted palette of earth pigments sourced from the volcanic soils around Mount Merapi, applied in thin, semi-transparent glazes. The surfaces are built up through dozens of layers, each modifying the perceptual field without fully obscuring what lies beneath. The effect is one of visual density that resists resolution into a stable image.

Critics have consistently described these works in relation to Merleau-Ponty's concept of the "flesh of the world," the idea that perception is not a representational act performed by a disembodied consciousness but a reciprocal exchange between the sensing body and the sensible world. Hartono's paintings do not depict surfaces so much as instantiate them. The layered glazes produce a material thickness that operates as an analogue for the phenomenological thickness of perception itself. What the viewer sees is not a picture of a landscape or a wall but a surface that has accumulated time and attention in a manner structurally homologous to the way the body accumulates experience.

Hartono's engagement with phenomenological philosophy was not merely illustrative. He did not paint "about" Merleau-Ponty. Rather, the philosophical texts provided him with a vocabulary for understanding what his practice was already doing, and that understanding in turn refined the practice. In a 1993 interview with the Indonesian art historian Sanento Yuliman, published posthumously in the journal "Seni" in 2023, Hartono described reading Husserl's lectures on internal time consciousness as a confirmation of something he had already grasped in the studio: that duration is not a container in which events occur but the very texture through which events become perceptible at all.

The 1980s saw Hartono expand into sculpture. His sculptural works, predominantly in cast bronze and carved teak, extend the phenomenological concerns of the paintings into three dimensions. "Berat Sendiri" (Own Weight, 1984), held in the collection of the National Gallery of Australia, consists of a bronze slab approximately two metres in height, its surface worked with chisel marks that follow no discernible pattern. The piece rests directly on the gallery floor without a plinth, a decision Hartono insisted upon in every exhibition. The work's title refers to the physical property of self-support, but it also carries the philosophical implication that the object's meaning is not imposed from without but emerges from its own material constitution. The viewer walking around the piece encounters a surface that changes character with every shift in position and lighting, refusing the gestalt coherence that conventional sculpture solicits.

Hartono's architectural commissions, fewer in number but significant in scale, apply the same principles to built form. The Pura Kehadiran, completed in 1992 on a site overlooking the Parangtritis coast south of Yogyakarta, is a private contemplative structure commissioned by a collective of Indonesian intellectuals and spiritual practitioners. The building consists of a single rectangular room with walls of packed earth and volcanic stone, lit only by a narrow clerestory running the full length of the north wall. There is no fixed focal point. The interior surfaces, left unfinished, record the marks of their construction. The architectural historian Jennifer Taylor, writing in her 2003 survey "An Architecture of Presence: Buildings of the Asia-Pacific Region", described the Pura Kehadiran as "a building that does not represent space but produces the experience of spatiality as such." Hartono designed only two further architectural works: a studio addition for the painter Nasir Baharudin in Penang, completed in 1998, and a memorial pavilion on the grounds of the Taman Ismail Marzuki cultural centre in Jakarta, completed in 2005.

Hartono's photographic work, less widely known than his painting and sculpture, occupies a distinctive place in his oeuvre. He began photographing in the mid-1980s, using a medium-format Rolleiflex camera he had purchased in Melbourne and carried with him on return visits to Australia. The photographs, almost without exception, are studies of surfaces: weathered walls in the kampung of Yogyakarta, the eroded facades of shophouses in Penang and Malacca, the cracked paving of the forecourt at the National Gallery of Victoria. They are not documentary images. Hartono printed them himself in small editions, manipulating exposure and development to produce tonal ranges that echo the glaze structures of his paintings. The photographs function as philosophical investigations in their own right, isolating the visual properties of surface, texture, and temporal accumulation that his work in other media explores through different means.

The relationship between Hartono's Australian and Southeast Asian contexts is central to understanding his contribution. He maintained studios in Yogyakarta and, from 1996, a smaller working space in Fitzroy, Melbourne, where he spent several months each year. His work was exhibited regularly in both contexts, and the critical reception differed in instructive ways. In Australia, where his paintings were shown at the National Gallery of Victoria in 1989 and the Art Gallery of New South Wales in 1995, critics tended to situate his work within the lineage of abstract tonalism and the broader discourse of international modernism. In Indonesia and Singapore, where his work was shown at the Cemeti Art House in Yogyakarta and the Singapore Art Museum, critics and curators placed greater emphasis on the local conditions of production: the volcanic pigments, the political history of the ASRI milieu, the specific textures of Javanese built environment that his surfaces evoke.

Hartono himself resisted the framing of his work as either Australian or Southeast Asian, insisting that the phenomenological concerns were not culturally specific. In a 2010 lecture at the University of Melbourne, later published in the anthology "Cross-Currents: Art and Philosophy in the Asia-Pacific", he said: "The body that perceives is not an Australian body or a Javanese body. It is a body. What it perceives is conditioned by where it stands, but the fact of standing, and the fact of perceiving through standing, is not conditional." The statement is characteristic of his rhetorical style: direct, slightly austere, and philosophically precise without conceding anything to jargon.

His teaching career, conducted primarily through informal studio apprenticeships in Yogyakarta rather than institutional appointments, shaped a generation of artists working across the region. Among his former students are the painters Entang Wiharso and Mella Jaarsma, and the sculptor F.X. Harsono, each of whom has acknowledged Hartono's influence on their approaches to material and perception. He held visiting positions at the Victorian College of the Arts in 1985 and at the University of Melbourne's School of Culture and Communication in 2002.

Hartono's late work, produced after 2010, is marked by a gradual simplification. The paintings become smaller, the surfaces thinner, the palettes more reduced. The final canvases, completed in 2021, measure approximately 30 by 40 centimetres and consist of no more than five or six layers of glaze. They are among the most radical statements of his career, reducing the phenomenological investigation to its minimum conditions. A selection of these late paintings was exhibited at the Singapore Art Museum in late 2022 in the exhibition "Permukaan Akhir" (Final Surface), which Hartono was able to attend despite declining health. A posthumous exhibition of the remaining late works, organised in collaboration with the National Gallery of Australia, is scheduled to open in Canberra in March 2024.

Hartono is survived by his wife, the textile artist Murtini Hartono, whom he married in 1972, their daughter Larasati Hartono, an architect practising in Melbourne, and two grandchildren. A memorial gathering will be held at the Cemeti Art House in Yogyakarta on a date to be announced. In lieu of flowers, the family has requested contributions to the Yogyakarta Studio Foundation, which supports emerging artists in the Bantul district.

The significance of Hartono's practice lies in the rigor with which he pursued a single set of questions across multiple media and more than half a century of work. Those questions, drawn from the phenomenological tradition and tested against the material realities of paint, bronze, stone, wood, and photographic emulsion, concern the nature of perception itself: how a surface becomes visible, how time becomes tangible, and how the body comes to know the world through the very act of looking. His answers, embodied in objects rather than arguments, remain among the most sustained and materially intelligent contributions to visual art's engagement with philosophy in the region.

**Issued by the Records and Heritage Office, City of Winnipeg, in consultation with the Manitoba Indigenous Cultural Education Centre**

## 1. Purpose

This Note establishes the standards governing municipal custody, description, and reproduction of sound recordings, transcriptions, and notated scores containing Indigenous-language song material. It applies to holdings of the City Archives, the Winnipeg Public Library local history collections, and materials received through the Public Art Program.

## 2. Scope of Affected Materials

The Office has identified 412 items falling within this Note, principally:

- Wax-cylinder and reel-to-reel recordings collected between 1902 and 1968, chiefly in **Anishinaabemowin (Ojibwe)**, **Nēhiyawēwin (Plains Cree)**, **Dakota**, and **Michif**;
- Hymn translations produced under mission auspices at St. Peter's and Norway House;
- Textile, beadwork, and painted items whose designs are documented as accompanying specific song cycles.

## 3. Governing Principles

**3.1 Songs are not uniformly public.** Certain items are ceremonial property held by named individuals, families, or societies. Their possession by the City does not constitute a right of use. Staff shall not assume that public-domain copyright status confers ethical permission to publish, broadcast, or exhibit.

**3.2 Language is substance, not metadata.** Titles and texts shall be rendered in the source language using standard orthography — Roman orthography or syllabics as appropriate — with English translation recorded as secondary. Prior catalogue entries reading "Indian song" or "native chant" are to be corrected as encountered.

**3.3 Provenance of collection matters.** Where a recording was obtained under residential-school authority, coerced circumstances, or without documented consent, that circumstance shall appear in the descriptive record.

## 4. Required Procedure

1. **Flag** any item within Section 2 upon accession or discovery.
2. **Refer** the item to the Heritage Office within ten business days.
3. **Consult** the relevant First Nation, Métis, or Inuit authority, working through the appropriate Treaty One community, the Manitoba Métis Federation, or Manitoba Keewatinowi Okimakanak.
4. **Restrict** access pending determination. Default status is closed, not open.
5. **Record** the determination, including any refusal to grant access, and the name and office of the person consulted.

## 5. Reproduction and Public Art

No Indigenous-language song text or associated visual motif shall be incorporated into a City commission, plaque, mural, or transit installation without written authorization from the originating community. Authorization for one use does not extend to subsequent uses.

Welcome to Harbor City, where three political parties are competing to steer the grand ship HMS Fair Vote. The Blue Party wants the fastest route, the Green Party wants cleaner sails, and the Yellow Party wants more lifeboats for everyone.

But Captain Iron has other plans. He announces that only one party may speak, elections are “too wobbly,” and every sailor must salute before breakfast. That is authoritarianism: power gathered by one leader or group, with little room for disagreement. Even a ship needs more than one person checking the compass.

Your mission is to solve the harbor puzzle. The security patrol reports three clues: the lighthouse is working, the harbor gate is locked, and the patrol boat has enough fuel. Which choice best protects the crew while keeping the ship free?

A. Let Captain Iron make every decision forever.
B. Allow elected officers, open debate, clear rules, and coast guard checks.
C. Give the loudest sailor the keys to the radio.

Correct answer: B. Strong security protects people from danger, but it should also protect their rights. On a well-run vessel, officers follow the law, crews can report problems, and no captain is above the rules. Now untie the lines—and keep your eyes on the compass.

Beloved colleagues in cultivation, we turn our attention to the ordering of creation, for the harvest is not gathered by chance alone but through the faithful application of universal laws. As the psalmist declares that the heavens declare the glory, so too does the furrow reveal the work of our hands when guided by knowledge. We approach the soil not as conquerors but as caretakers, and our instruction today concerns the tools of that stewardship: the measure, the element, and the living breath.

Consider first the burden of Mathematics, which the ancients recognized as the language of proportion. When we calculate the yield per hectare or determine the precise ratio of seed to acreage, we participate in an ordering principle that transcends our individual desires. The algebra of the feed ration, the geometry of the irrigation channel, the calculus of seasonal growth curves—these are not mere administrative tasks but disciplines of humility, reminding us that excess and deficiency alike lead to ruin. The ledger book is a book of reckonings, and those who would feed the multitudes must first master the integrity of the column.

We turn then to Chemistry, that invisible commerce between earth and plant. The nitrogen cycle is a testament to transformation, a perpetual dying and rising that sustains all flesh. When we apply amendments to depleted soil, we engage in a sacred trust: to restore what has been withdrawn, to balance the pH as a steward balances accounts. The synthesis of fertilizers, the composition of pesticides, the analysis of tissue samples—these require precision, for the difference between remedy and poison lies in concentration. We handle the elemental forces of creation, and our mandate is not domination but restoration.

Biology instructs us in the interdependence of the living. The organism is not an isolated unit but a participant in an ecosystem of mutual dependence. From the microbiology of the rhizosphere to the population dynamics of the herd, we observe systems of resilience and vulnerability. The integrated pest management strategy, the breeding program designed for disease resistance, the rotational grazing plan—these acknowledge that our authority over creation is bounded by the inherent needs of the creatures themselves. We do not create life; we arrange the conditions under which it flourishes.

Finally, we must account for Pollution, the consequence of our fallibility. The runoff that contaminates the watershed, the chemical residue that accumulates in the food chain, the erosion that silts the streams—these bear witness to our failure of proportion. The nitrogen and phosphorus loads in the Chesapeake Bay, the hypoxic zones in the Gulf, the groundwater contamination beneath our very counties—these are the costs of practices that prioritized yield over stewardship. Our task now is remediation: buffer strips along waterways, precision application technologies, and the restoration of wetland filtration systems. We must atone for the imbalance, not through abdication, but through the rigorous application of the very sciences that revealed our error.

Go forth and study, for the world awaits your careful hands.

HOST:

We're talking today with Maria Chen, who tracks supply chain patterns for outdoor recreation companies. Maria, you've been looking at how sporting goods actually reach people in the mountains. What surprised you most?

MARIA:

The biggest surprise was learning how much still moves through independent retailers rather than chains. I expected Amazon and Dick's Sporting Goods to dominate, but in counties across eastern Kentucky and West Virginia, you've still got these family-run shops that have been there thirty, forty years. They're the ones stocking fishing tackle, hunting licenses, climbing gear.

HOST:

So these aren't just nostalgia operations.

MARIA:

Not at all. They're positioned perfectly for logistics. A warehouse in Charlotte can't service a town of 800 people efficiently. But a local shop owner knows exactly what families need, knows the seasons, knows which trails people actually use. They're getting shipments from regional distributors who understand Appalachian geography in ways the national logistics networks don't.

HOST:

Does that affect pricing?

MARIA:

Interestingly, no. Local retailers often match online prices because their costs are lower. They're not paying for last-mile delivery infrastructure. What they're really selling is immediacy and local knowledge. You can't get that from an algorithm.

O Unmoved Mover, First and Final State,

I come before You in the isolated system of my heart, where no work crosses the boundary and no heat escapes unaccounted. Grant me the patience of reversible processes, that I might approach Your inefficiency without the entropy of haste.

The First Law You inscribed: energy neither created nor destroyed, only transformed. In this I trust when my own internal energy depletes, when the work of days exhausts my capacity for heat exchange with the world. Let my enthalpy remain sufficient to the reactions You require of me.

Yet I tremble before the Second Law, Lord of increase. All real processes irreversible. All organized forms trending toward uniform distribution. The heat death waits at the end of every engine cycle, every metabolic pathway, every stellar burning. My own body runs at finite efficiency, wasting more than it utilizes, contributing its measure to the universal entropy.

Still You established the constants: Boltzmann's bridge between macrostate and microstate, Planck's quantum of action, the fixed speed of light that bounds all information transfer. These do not change. These I cling to.

Let my free energy be spent purposefully. Let my activation barriers be surmountable. When equilibrium comes, as it must, may the universe have grown more complex in its disorder, more interesting in its dissipation, more worthy of the initial conditions You set at time's beginning.

In the name of the Hamiltonian, the Lagrangian, and the invariant interval, amen.

ENTERED INTO this day by the duly authorized representatives of the undersigned sovereign peoples, in recognition of the imperishable worth of the languages, arts, and historical traditions transmitted from antiquity to the present generation;

WHEREAS the civilizations of antiquity, from the valley of the Nile to the banks of the Tigris, from the marble precincts of Hellas to the forums of the Eternal City, erected monuments of language and art which endure as the common inheritance of humankind; and

WHEREAS the successive empires and kingdoms of the medieval and early modern epochs — the courts of Byzantium, the caliphates of Córdoba and Baghdad, the principalities of the Sahel, the dynasties of the Indus and the Hwang Ho — each contributed distinct tongues, scripts, and aesthetic traditions to the treasury of nations; and

WHEREAS the wars and upheavals of the past four centuries have, in many instances, placed these heritages in peril through destruction, displacement, and the abandonment of living practice;

NOW, THEREFORE, the Signatory Nations do hereby covenant and agree as follows:

I. DEFINITIONS
For the purposes of this instrument, the term "Endangered Language" shall denote any natural language, whether classical or vernacular, presently spoken by fewer than ten thousand persons or restricted to ceremonial and ritual use. The term "Heritage Art" shall encompass all material and performative works whose techniques, iconography, or forms derive from traditions continuous with those of pre-modern civilizations.

II. OBLIGATIONS OF PRESERVATION
Each Signatory shall establish, within its own territories, a national registry of Endangered Languages spoken by communities within its borders, and shall take reasonable measures, through public instruction and recognized orthographies, to ensure their continued transmission to successive generations. Where a tongue is shared across frontiers, the parties shall consult concerning the unification of scholarly standards and the free exchange of pedagogical materials.

III. PROTECTION OF HERITAGE ART
The Signatories acknowledge the principle that monuments, manuscripts, and works of art, wherever situated, form part of the patrimony of all peoples. Each party undertakes to restrain the illicit excavation, exportation, and sale of objects removed from the lands wherein they were created, and to facilitate, upon proper application, the return of such objects to their place of origin.

IV. COOPERATION IN SCHOLARSHIP
The parties shall encourage the translation of foundational texts — including legal, literary, and scientific treatises composed in the ancient and medieval languages — into the working languages of the Signatories, and shall promote the compilation of lexicons, grammars, and concordances necessary to the advancement of learning.

V. DURATION AND AMENDMENT
This treaty shall remain in force for a term of fifty years and shall be renewed thereafter by mutual consent. Amendments may be proposed by any Signatory and shall take effect upon ratification by two-thirds of the parties.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the representatives aforesaid have hereunto set their hands and seals, in the year of our common era Two Thousand and Twenty-Four.

Along the Ohio River, morning bells arise,
From Cleveland docks to Cincinnati skies.
The Coast Guard cutter leaves the pier,
With charts, provisions, purpose clear.

No captain owns the river’s name,
No flag may turn the law to flame.
The people choose, the records show,
How public ships and services flow.

Hoist the colors, steady and bright,
A nation held by equal right.
From Toledo’s lakefront, west to east,
Let duty guide both ship and feast.

The harbor master checks each line,
The crews report at closing time.
A public trust is not command
By one unchecked and lifted hand.

When rulers silence every voice,
And make obedience the only choice,
The strongest hull may split apart,
For fear cannot secure a heart.

Our strength is found in work made plain:
Safe channels, bridges, locks, and rain;
In budgets read and duties shared,
In every watch and life prepared.

So sail, Ohio, under skies
Where law and liberty can rise.
Let nationalism serve the shore,
Not ask the people to adore.

From river bend to Lake Erie,
Keep government both firm and free.
With open books and watchful eyes,
The common good shall steer our ties.
