body: this collection of high-resolution aerial photographs and annotated topography maps captures the industrial deposition patterns along the Rhine River valley between Duisburg and Koblenz. The images were taken during a series of low-altitude passes conducted in early spring, when reduced foliation allows clearer delineation of ground-level disturbances. Notations mark sediment plumes from steelworks in Duisburg, chemical plant effluents near Leverkusen, and legacy mining tailings around Bonn. The set includes stereoscopic pairs for 3D terrain modeling, with particular emphasis on meltwater drainage pathways carrying heavy metals into the floodplain. Taken at 5 cm/pixel resolution, the survey provides baseline data for tracking sediment transport in one of Europe’s most heavily industrialized waterways. The accompanying overlay sheets denote pH levels, particulate counts, and heavy metal concentrations corresponding to visual markers in the images. The survey was commissioned by the German Federal Environment Agency as part of ongoing monitoring under the EU Water Framework Directive.

Continuing education units (CEUs) are available for participants completing the full series; partial credit is granted for individual sessions at a rate of one CEU per three contact hours.

Registration is required for the October 23 and December 2 sessions due to room capacity. All other events operate on a drop-in basis, though advance notice helps us prepare materials appropriately.

Sessions will be held in person unless otherwise indicated. Should university operations be modified due to weather or other circumstances, updates will be posted to the Faculty Development portal and circulated by departmental email by 6:00 AM on the day of the event.

Reasonable accommodations are available upon request. Please contact the Office of Faculty Affairs at least five business days before any session you plan to attend so that appropriate arrangements can be made. ASL interpretation, large-print materials, and captioning services have all been arranged for previous workshops and can be provided again as needed.

Parking is available in the East Lot for evening sessions; daytime attendees should use their regular permits. A valid university ID is required for building access after 5:00 PM.

This series is sponsored by the Office of the Provost, the Department of Educational Psychology, and the Faculty Association. Questions may be directed to the Faculty Development Coordinator during regular business hours.

We look forward to your participation this semester.

Twenty years ago, the first trade delegation from Tokyo arrived in Springfield, marking the beginning of a partnership that would reshape commerce in both regions. Today, we honor the vision of those early collaborators—policymakers, business leaders, and academics—who recognized the mutual benefit of bridging Illinois’s industrial strength with Tokyo’s technological innovation.

The numbers speak to the success: bilateral trade has grown by 320% since 2004, with Illinois now serving as Japan’s leading agricultural supplier in the Midwest. Tokyo-based firms employ over 12,000 workers across our state, while Illinois manufacturers supply critical components to Japan’s automotive and electronics sectors. Public policy played a pivotal role, from tax incentives to streamlined customs agreements, ensuring this relationship flourished beyond mere transactional exchange.

Yet the true impact lies in the intangibles—the knowledge transfer, the cultural exchange, and the shared commitment to sustainable growth. As we reflect on this milestone, we also look ahead, mindful of emerging challenges in global supply chains and the need for adaptive policy frameworks.

To the architects of this partnership, we extend our deepest gratitude. Your foresight has not only strengthened economies but also fostered enduring ties between our communities. Here’s to the next twenty years of progress.

The Department of Geography and Anthropology mourns the passing of Dr. Margaret Halstead, whose contributions to the study of urban spatial cognition transformed our understanding of how Chicagoans navigate and interpret their city. For thirty-two years, Dr. Halstead guided students through the intricate relationship between psychological perception and geographic behavior, demonstrating that maps represent not merely physical space but the mental frameworks through which individuals construct their environments.

Her landmark 1989 study of neighborhood boundary perception among South Side residents revealed how psychological attachment shapes spatial practice, work that fundamentally challenged prevailing models of urban mobility. She brought equal rigor to her documentation of recreational traditions along the lakefront, recognizing that the weekend volleyball games at North Avenue Beach constituted a living laboratory for observing group dynamics and territorial behavior.

Dr. Halstead's fieldwork methods became standard practice: she insisted that students participate in the activities they studied. Her own participation in the Chinatown Lions Club dragon boat races and her years coaching youth soccer in Hyde Park embodied her belief that geographic knowledge emerges through embodied experience rather than detached observation.

The Halstead Laboratory for Spatial Cognition continues her work. A memorial gathering will be held at the Quadrangle Club on March 15th. In lieu of flowers, the family requests contributions to the field research scholarship fund established in her name.

body:
## Overview

Public higher education systems in the United States have navigated decades of fiscal restructuring, shifting enrollment demographics, and evolving mandates regarding the humanities. Two state university systems—the University of California (UC) and the California State University (CSU) on the West Coast, alongside Michigan's public institutions clustered around the University of Michigan, Michigan State University, Wayne State University, and the state's regional comprehensives—offer instructive contrasts in the financing of humanities departments and the cultural curricular frameworks those budgets sustain. This handbook compiles enrollment data, appropriations histories, and program-level funding mechanisms for scholars researching the political economy of humanities instruction at American state universities between 1990 and 2023.

## I. The Structural Context: Governance and Revenue Architecture

### California

The UC system operates as a constitutionally autonomous entity with a three-part funding model: state General Fund appropriations, tuition and fees, and external research grants and philanthropic gifts. From the 1990s onward, California's Proposition 98 (1988) guaranteed K–14 funding but did not extend comparable protections to the UC and CSU, leaving the senior higher education segment exposed to cyclical budget reductions.

The CSU system, the largest four-year public university in the country by enrollment, depends more heavily on state appropriations relative to tuition. CSU's historical "67/33" compact—an implicit agreement that the state would cover roughly two-thirds of educational costs—eroded substantially after the 2008 fiscal crisis and was effectively abandoned in the 2011–12 budget cycle. Per-student General Fund support at CSU fell from approximately $10,600 in 2007–08 to under $6,000 by 2012–13, in inflation-adjusted terms.

### Michigan

Michigan's structure diverges sharply. The University of Michigan, as a public-but-independent institution under a constitutionally chartered Board of Regents, draws a smaller proportion of its operating budget from the state than do the UC or CSU systems. State appropriations to UM-Ann Arbor constituted approximately 14 percent of general fund revenues in the early 2020s, down from roughly 50 percent in the early 1970s.

The Michigan State University and Wayne State University appropriations picture is more comparable to UC's—though MSU's land-grant mission (Morrill Act 1862) secures federal capacity funds, Hatch Act agricultural research dollars, and Smith-Lever cooperative extension allocations that have no analog in California's humanities-dominant units. The state's fifteen public universities are coordinated through the Michigan Association of State Universities, with no systemwide governance authority comparable to the UC Office of the President.

## II. Appropriations Volatility and the Humanities

Budget cuts to public higher education in both states have historically fallen most heavily on units lacking external grant revenue, clinical income, or athletic revenue streams. Humanities departments—English, history, philosophy, classics, comparative literature, area studies—rarely generate indirect cost recovery, patent income, or tuition premiums associated with professional schools.

### California Case Patterns

During the 2009–2012 contraction, UC and CSU humanities departments absorbed a disproportionate share of furlough days and lecturer reductions. UC Berkeley's Department of English saw its tenure-line faculty shrink from 49 to 39 between 2008 and 2014; UCLA's humanities units underwent comparable contraction. CSU campuses, operating under enrollment-funded rather than seat-funded budget models, were particularly vulnerable: Humboldt State's Department of Critical Race, Gender & Sexuality Studies and San José State's Humanities Department each experienced reductions exceeding 15 percent in tenure-track lines over the same period.

The 2020 COVID-era "interruption" funding—an emergent mechanism unique to California's pandemic response—included $1.7 billion in one-time allocations to UC and CSU specifically tied to enrollment continuity rather than to program-level protection. Humanities units benefited only indirectly, insofar as overall institutional stability preserved their positions.

### Michigan Case Patterns

Michigan's humanities contraction traced a different timeline. The state's 2007–2009 fiscal crisis produced a 15 percent reduction in per-student appropriations to MSU, Wayne State, and the University of Michigan-Flint. UM-Ann Arbor, drawing on its $17 billion endowment (as of 2023), was largely insulated from state-level cuts and in fact expanded humanities tenure lines during this period—particularly in African American Studies, Women's and Gender Studies, and Middle East Studies, funded substantially through the Gerald R. Ford School, the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, and external foundation gifts.

MSU's humanities units fared less well. College of Arts and Letters tenure density declined from 256 tenure-line faculty in 2007 to 198 by 2017. The closure of MSU's humanities programs would have been more severe absent the college's success in capturing Title VI funding for area studies centers—a federal revenue stream that protects curriculum in languages and area studies but does not subsidize general humanities instruction.

## III. Cultural Pedagogy and Curriculum Finance

### Area Studies and the Title VI Mechanism

Both states' flagship campuses house federally funded National Resource Centers under Title VI of the Higher Education Act. UC Berkeley, UCLA, and the University of Michigan each host multiple centers—Berkeley's Centers for Southeast Asia, Latin American Studies, and European Studies; Michigan's Center for Southeast Asian Studies, Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and Center for Russian, East European, and Eurasian Studies. These centers generate curricular resources, language instruction, and overseas research opportunities but operate on a federal appropriations cycle largely insulated from state fiscal volatility.

### Ethnic Studies Mandates

California's 2021–22 implementation of ethnic studies graduation requirements (AB 1460, 2020) created a unique financial-cultural pressure point. UC and CSU were required to offer courses meeting approved ethnic studies criteria for all undergraduates, but no commensurate General Fund augmentation accompanied the mandate. CSU campuses reported needing to hire 50–80 additional lecturers systemwide to meet demand; UC estimated $25–35 million in annual implementation costs across its nine undergraduate campuses.

Michigan has no comparable statutory requirement. Wayne State University, located in Detroit, has maintained a robust African American Studies program since the 1970s as part of its urban mission, but ethnic studies proliferation at Michigan's other publics has proceeded through departmental initiative rather than legislative mandate. MSU's James Madison College and Residential College in the Arts and Humanities (RCAH) provide alternative curricular homes for interdisciplinary cultural studies.

### Cross-Campus Collaborative Funding

The Big Ten Academic Alliance (formerly CIC) provides a distinctive infrastructure for Michigan humanities collaboration: shared library access, course-sharing arrangements, and the Committee on Institutional Cooperation's humanities-focused fellowships. California lacks a comparable consortium-wide humanities mechanism. The UC Humanities Network, formally established in 2010, facilitates research collaboration and grant pursuit but does not redistribute instructional resources across campuses.

## IV. Tuition, Fees, and the Privatization Trajectory

Both states' public universities have moved along a continuum of privatization—shifting revenue from state appropriations to tuition, fees, and auxiliary enterprises. UC's undergraduate tuition rose from $4,564 in 2000–01 to $14,253 in 2023–24 for in-state students (nominal dollars). Michigan's public universities, particularly MSU and Wayne State, experienced comparable trajectories, though UM-Ann Arbor's tuition ($16,378 in-state for 2023–24) reflects its independent budget profile.

Supplementary fees supporting cultural and co-curricular programming—language labs, performing arts facilities, museum operations—appear in both systems' unit-level budgets but rarely as protected line items. UC Berkeley's Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, UCLA's Fowler Museum, and the University of Michigan Museum of Art (now the UMMA) each rely on hybrid funding models combining university general funds, endowment income, gift revenue, and earned income. During fiscal contractions, museum hours, acquisitions budgets, and educational programming are typically the first to be reduced.

## V. Comparative Summary Table

| Dimension | UC System | CSU System | University of Michigan | MSU / Wayne State |
|-----------|-----------|------------|------------------------|-------------------|
| State share of general fund (2023) | ~12% | ~34% | ~14% | ~25% |
| Endowment per FTE (2023) | ~$45,000 | ~$8,000 | ~$370,000 | ~$25,000 |
| Title VI NRCs | 14 (across system) | 2 | 6 | 3 |
| Ethnic studies mandate | Yes (AB 1460) | Yes (AB 1460) | No | No |
| Tenure density in humanities (2017 index) | 0.78 of 2007 | 0.71 of 2007 | 0.95 of 2007 | 0.77 of 2007 |

*Tenure density figures normalized to 2007 baseline; FTE enrollment adjusted.*

## VI. Methodological Notes for Researchers

Scholars pursuing comparative work on this topic should note several data caveats. The Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) provides consistent revenue and expenditure reporting, but functional expenditure breakdowns by discipline are not systematically captured. Departmental-level budget data are typically treated as internal records at UC and CSU; FOIA requests to the UC Office of the President and to individual CSU chancellor's offices have yielded usable longitudinal data for specific humanities departments since approximately 2015.

In Michigan, the Michigan Association of State Universities and Universities Research Corridor provides publicly available aggregated data, but individual department figures remain more opaque than at UC. Researchers should anticipate a two- to four-month FOIA response timeline.

For cultural pedagogy analyses, course catalog archives are essential. UC's historical course catalogs are searchable through the California Digital Library; Michigan's are accessible through the individual university libraries and through Archive.org's regional collection.

## VII. Funding Recommendation for Future Scholarship

Three priority areas warrant further documentation. First, the interaction between Title VI center funding and host-institution curricular commitments, particularly the extent to which federal funding substitutes for what would otherwise be state-supported instruction. Second, the differential impact of ethnic studies mandates on humanities curricular structure, comparing California's AB 1460 effect with Michigan's voluntary adoption patterns. Third, the role of auxiliary and gift revenue in insulating museum-based cultural pedagogy from state appropriations volatility—a phenomenon observable in both UC Berkeley's BAM/PFA and UMMA, but with sharply different institutional accounting treatments.

Researchers with access to departmental general ledgers, course enrollment files, and tenure density counts at the unit level should prioritize collaboration with state university archivists in both systems, who have begun systematic digitization of internal budget records with attention to long-term preservation.

Mrs. Pemberton's eight-by-six-foot garden shed has become the unlikely centerpiece of a three-year planning dispute with Rushmore District Council. What began as a simple extension to her Cotswolds property evolved into a masterclass in how administrative law can transform a modest structure into a matter of constitutional significance.

The council's initial refusal cited breach of permitted development rights under the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995. Mrs. Pemberton appealed, arguing the shed qualified as an ancillary building. The planning inspector disagreed. She appealed again. The council reconsidered. A second inspector found the distinction between "ancillary" and "incidental" insufficiently clear in precedent. Meanwhile, the shed remained standing.

What makes this case instructive is not the shed itself but the machinery it set in motion. Mrs. Pemberton exhausted every administrative remedy available: written representations, oral hearings, judicial review applications, and correspondence with her MP. Each stage revealed the byzantine pathways through which property owners must navigate when discretionary decisions meet statutory frameworks.

The eventual resolution came not through the courts but through a planning permission granted on fresh application, rendering the entire administrative odyssey moot. The shed stands today, legally sanctioned at last, a monument to the proposition that in administrative law, the journey often matters more than the destination.

**1. Defining the Resource**

Cultural resources in California contexts broadly encompass built environment, traditional cultural properties, and (where applicable) archaeological loci. When evaluating a property listed in or eligible for the California Register, consultants typically assess integrity of location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, feeling, and association. For the National Register, the bar is higher — Criterion Consideration G ordinarily disqualishes properties less than 50 years old unless exceptional significance is documented.

**2. Survey Methodology**

Intensive-level survey should follow a grid pattern at 15-meter intervals in areas of low slope and visibility, tightening to 5 meters near previously recorded isolates or in zones flagged by the**California Historical Resources Information System (CHRIS)**. Native American consultation under**Assembly Bill 52 (2014)** — reissued through amended Public Resources Code § 21080.3 — is required for projects affecting tribal cultural resources; the California Office of Historic Preservation and the Native American Heritage Commission, Sacramento office, should both be contacted early. Sacred Lands Inventory searches are mandatory prior to fieldwork authorization.

**3. Built Environment and Historic Districts**

Documentation should reference**Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) 523** Primary and Continuation forms (A through K). In urban contexts — Sacramento, Los Angeles, San Francisco —**period of significance** typically anchors 1870–1940, with postwar subdivisions (1945–1970) warranting preliminary evaluation under recent guidance.

**4. Curation**

Recovered materials must be curated at a facility meeting**36 CFR Part 79** standards, with the**California Statewide Chipped Stone Database** consulted for chronometric comparisons when lithic assemblages are involved.

Law schools across the Southeast Asian region and throughout North Carolina have long treated literature and commerce as separate intellectual territories, each with its own casebooks, its own pedagogical traditions, and its own unspoken assumption that they have little to teach each other. Yet a growing body of scholarship suggests this disciplinary segregation may be counterproductive, particularly for students preparing to practice commercial law.

Consider the teaching potential of Charles Dickens's "Bleak House," a novel that, as legal scholar James Boyd White has argued, functions as an extended meditation on the failure of contractual systems (White, 1973). The Jarndyce v. Jarndyce suit—a Chancery case that consumes fortunes and decades—operates less as narrative ornament than as a structural principle for understanding how legal language can obscure rather than clarify intent. When teaching the doctrine of consideration or the parol evidence rule, why not pair these doctrinal materials with the novel's depiction of how parties to litigation become trapped by the very language meant to govern their relationship?

Several law faculties in the Research Triangle have begun experimenting with this integration. At Duke Law School, for instance, some contracts professors have incorporated excerpts from nineteenth-century commercial fiction to illustrate formation problems and course of dealing disputes. The pedagogical rationale is straightforward: literature dramatizes the human stakes of contractual ambiguity in ways that appellate opinions, by their nature, often obscure.

The benefits appear threefold. First, students develop what might be termed contractual literacy—the ability to recognize how language functions persuasively and ambiguously simultaneously. Second, exposure to literary representations of commerce cultivates what some legal educators call "contextual awareness," the recognition that contracts exist within social, economic, and psychological contexts that formal doctrine alone cannot capture (Sternlight, 2014). Third, and perhaps most pragmatically, law students who have engaged seriously with commercial literature often demonstrate improved performance on drafting assignments, suggesting that close reading of non-doctrinal texts strengthens the interpretive skills that underlie effective legal writing.

Whether this approach constitutes genuine pedagogical innovation or merely a sophisticated distraction remains contested. Some faculty members worry that literary analysis dilutes the efficiency of doctrinal instruction. Yet as legal education continues to confront questions about how best to prepare graduates for practice contexts that demand not only technical knowledge but also interpretive sophistication, the case for occasional literary detours grows incrementally stronger.

The relationship between linguistic structure and tonal aesthetics in sacred organ repertory presents a recurring analytical challenge, particularly when evaluating how specific registrations serve doctrinal text-setting. Consider the French Classic organ school: the Plein Jeu manualiter operates not merely as acoustic foregrounding but as a semantic enhancer for Credo intonations, where the harmonic series reinforces theological claims of divine transcendence through sounds inherently upward-striving partial structure.

This correspondence extends into comparative liturgical traditions. The seventeen-century North German organ-building aesthetic—exemplified in the Schnitger organs of Hamburg and Lübeck—favors a brighter, more speech-like plenum. The articulation of thePrincipal chorus aligns directly with the syllabic demands of Lutheran chorale textures, while French practice, by contrast, employs the cornet séparé to vowel-like elongation in motet-style verse settings.

Composers leverage these timbral-linguistic equivalences to dramatic effect. In Franck's Choral No. 3 in A minor, the interior dialogue between the Voix céleste and foundational pedal trombone functions as a structural representation of contested spiritual states—beauty as seductive masking the requirement for resolution. The instrument ceases to function merely as a vehicle for melody but becomes a didactic instrument.

For the analyst, effective work in this area requires parsing multiple concurrent grammars: verbal syntax, harmonic syntax, and the syntactical implications of registration. Tools from semiotics—particularly the index-icon-symbol triad—illuminate how the organ, alone among instruments, simultaneously references textual meaning, represents affective states, and embodies a tradition where acoustic beauty and theological truth claims remain inseparably bound.

A working file for the Marseille commission, focusing on the intersection of sacred music traditions and contemporary congregational life in Provence.

The project centers on documenting evening Vespers at the Basilique Notre-Dame de la Garde and the sung Offices at the Abbaye Saint-Victor, both in Marseille. We are working toward a visual essay that traces how Gregorian and Provençal liturgical musical traditions persist, fragment, and reconstitute themselves within living congregational practice. The aim is not archival preservation — that work has been done — but rather a philosophical and cultural reading of how sound shapes communal religious identity in a secularized European context.

Shooting will take place over four consecutive evenings in late October. We have obtained permission from Father Bertin and the Abbot's office, with the understanding that no artificial lighting will be introduced and that the community's sung prayer remains the controlling rhythm of all visual decisions. Equipment is minimal: two bodies, fast primes only, no rigs. We are looking for the gesture of breath before chant, the posture of waiting between antiphons, the way candlelight reorganizes a face mid-phrase.

Ethically, we are guests at prayer, not observers of spectacle. The community knows we are present. If a communicant signals discomfort, we stop. Review footage on site each night; we will not have a second opportunity. Deliverables are a forty-minute cut and approximately sixty still frames, captioned in French and English, for the diocesan cultural office and festival submission.

I. PARTIES

This Memorandum is entered into between the Department of Education of the State of Florida, herein "the Department," and the undersigned contracting provider of curricular services, herein "the Provider," whose registered office is situated in Miami-Dade County, Florida, and whose activities extend to consultative arrangements with bodies within England and Wales.

II. PURPOSE

The parties acknowledge a shared interest in the development of sociology as a discrete area of instruction within secondary education, and in the equitable treatment of teaching staff engaged in its delivery.

III. SCOPE OF WORK

The Provider shall design, prepare, and deliver teaching materials addressing sociological concepts, including but not limited to social stratification, labour relations, and the structure of institutions. Materials shall be benchmarked, where practicable, against comparable units of study offered at Key Stage 5 in England, and shall reflect accepted academic conventions in the discipline.

IV. LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT

All instruction shall be carried out by qualified persons fairly compensated in accordance with the laws of Florida and applicable federal standards of the United States. Working conditions shall conform to statutory requirements concerning hours, rest, and remuneration.

Compensation shall be as set forth in Schedule A, attached.

VI. TERM

This Memorandum shall remain in force for one (1) academic year, renewable upon mutual written agreement.

VII. GOVERNING LAW

This instrument shall be governed by the laws of the State of Florida. Cross-reference to United Kingdom frameworks is for academic alignment only.

Welcome aboard, junior captains! Today's mission is to steer our ship through the tricky waters of Harbor Bay, where three colorful party boats are arguing over the best route. The Red Team wants to go fast, the Blue Team prefers a slow scan, and the Green Team insists on zig-zagging to visit every island. Your job is to solve this floating puzzle by finding the one path that keeps everyone safe without letting any single boat take the wheel completely. Watch out for the foggy zone ahead; if one captain tries to shout down the others and force a dangerous shortcut, the whole fleet could crash into the rocky cliffs of Dictator Island.

Remember, a strong navy and a brave coast guard work best when they follow rules made together, not orders from just one boss who refuses to listen. In our game, if you see a leader locking the map room or silencing the lookouts, that is a sign to drop your anchor immediately. True security comes from checking compasses with friends and making sure no single flag flies higher than the safety of the crew. Use your decoder ring to match the right compromise to each storm cloud, ensuring that every voice on the bridge helps guide the ship home. Once you connect the dots between listening, sharing, and staying alert, you will unlock the secret code to peace in the bay. Grab your crayons and chart the course that keeps freedom afloat for sailors of all ages.

The Town of Chestnut Ridge Recreation Department, located at 273 South Madison Avenue, operates seventeen parks, four swimming facilities, and twelve miles of hiking trails throughout the 2024 summer season. WILDLIFE ADVISORY: CASCADE LAKE PARK AND MILLBROOK NATURE CENTER

The Town of Chestnut Ridge contains significant natural areas within the Lower Hudson Valley ecological region. These areas support diverse wildlife populations that vary seasonally. Residents and visitors should be aware of wildlife activity when using recreational facilities.

MAMMALS RECORDED IN TOWN PARKS

White-tailed Deer (Odocoileus virginianus)
Population estimate: 38 deer per square mile in developed areas; 52 per square mile in Cascade Lake corridor
Activity: Crepuscular (dawn and dusk); most active May through June (fawning season) and October through November (mating season)
Advisory: Do not approach fawns found alone; does frequently leave young unattended while foraging. Report injured deer to Environmental Conservation Officer dispatch at 877-457-5680.
Vehicle collisions peak November through December; use caution on Cascade Lake Road and Pine Grove Road during evening hours.

Eastern Coyote (Canis latrans)
Population estimate: 3-4 family groups across Town; primary territory centered on Millbrook Nature Center and adjacent watershed lands
Activity: Primarily nocturnal; may be active during daylight in uninhabited areas
Advisory: Coyotes are established throughout Rockland County and present minimal risk to humans. Secure garbage containers and remove bird feeders if coyotes are observed. Report aggressive behavior or animals approaching humans to Police Department at 845-356-9700.
Domestic pets should be supervised; cats and small dogs should not be left outdoors unattended at dawn, dusk, or overnight.

Red Fox (Vulpes vulpes)
Population estimate: 8-12 individuals across fragmented territories
Activity: Crepuscular; denning occurs March through May
Advisory: Foxes commonly observed near Veterans Memorial Pool and Community Center. Do not feed; habituated animals may become aggressive. Report foxes exhibiting no fear of humans or appearing sick (staggering, loss of coordination) to Rockland County Department of Health at 845-364-2592.

Eastern Cottontail Rabbit (Sylvilagus floridanus)
Population estimate: Abundant; population cycles every 7-10 years
Activity: Crepuscular year-round
Advisory: Primary prey species for local predator populations. No specific precautions required.

Woodchuck (Marmota monax)
Population estimate: 40+ burrow systems identified; actual population unknown
Activity: Diurnal; hibernation November through February
Activity: Burrows present in open areas throughout all parks. Avoid burrow entrances; provide habitat for additional species includingEastern box turtles and small mammals.

Virginia Opossum (Didelphis virginiana)
Population estimate: Moderate and stable
Activity: Nocturnal
Advisory: North America's only marsupial. Generally non-aggressive; may "play dead" when threatened. Beneficial for tick control (estimated consumption of 5,000+ ticks per season per individual).

Raccoon (Procyon lotor)
Population estimate: High density in developed areas adjacent to parks
Activity: Nocturnal; most active summer months
Advisory: Primary rabies vector species in Rockland County. Do not approach; report animals active during daylight hours or showing signs of illness to Health Department. Secure all garbage in wildlife-proof containers.

BIRDS RECORDED IN TOWN PARKS

Mute Swan (Cygnus olor)
Population: 4 resident pairs on Cascade Lake; 2 nests identified in 2024
Activity: Year-round residents
Advisory: Extremely aggressive during nesting (April through June) and while protecting cygnets. Maintain minimum 100-foot distance from adults and nests. Nesting areas marked with signage; avoid marked coves.

Canada Goose (Branta canadensis)
Population: 150+ resident birds; 400+ during migration (March-April, October-November)
Activity: Year-round residents with migratory augmentation
Advisory: Aggressive during nesting (March through May). Droppings contribute to water quality concerns at Cascade Lake swimming areas; avoid feeding. Federal protection under Migratory Bird Treaty Act; nests and eggs may not be disturbed.

Wild Turkey (Meleagris gallopavo)
Population: Estimated 75-100 birds in flocks throughout Town
Activity: Diurnal; roosts in trees overnight
Advisory: Occasionally aggressive during breeding season (March through May). If turkeys display aggressive behavior, make noise and appear large; do not run. Report aggressive individuals to Recreation office.

Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis)
Population: 6-8 breeding pairs with established territories
Activity: Diurnal
Advisory: Nests located in mature trees throughout park system. Nesting occurs March through June; avoid areas under active nests to prevent abandonment. Federally protected.

Great Horned Owl (Bubo virginianus)
Population: 3-4 breeding territories in Town parks
Activity: Nocturnal
Advisory: Established nests near Millbrook Nature Center and Cascade Lake eastern shore. No specific precautions; enjoy listening for nighttime calls.

Waterfowl (Various Species)
Cascade Lake supports resident populations of Mallards, Wood Ducks, and Double-crested Cormorants. Migratory species observed during spring and fall include Common Loon, various grebes, and waterfowl. Birding opportunities best March through May and September through November.

REPTILES AND AMPHIBIANS

Eastern Box Turtle (Terrapene carolina carolina)
Status: Species of Special Concern in New York State
Population: Unknown; documented in Millbrook Nature Center and Cascade Lake Park
Advisory: Slow-moving; frequently crossing trails May through June and September. Watch for turtles on trails; observe but do not relocate. Found injured turtles may be taken to wildlife rehabilitator (contact Recreation office for list).

Snapping Turtle (Chelydra serpentina)
Population: Common in Cascade Lake and associated wetlands
Activity: Most visible June through July during nesting season
Advisory: Females travel up to 1 mile from water to lay eggs. Cross roads and trails during nesting; use caution when driving near aquatic habitats. DO NOT HANDLE; powerful bite can cause serious injury. If turtle is on road, safely pull over and allow it to cross; do not pick up.

Eastern Garter Snake (Thamnophis sirtalis)
Population: Abundant throughout all park facilities
Activity: Diurnal, April through October
Advisory: Common non-venomous snake frequently observed in grass and near water. No threat to humans; beneficial for insect control.

Northern Water Snake (Nerodia sipedon)
Population: Common in Cascade Lake and ponds
Activity: Diurnal; often basking on rocks and logs near water
Advisory: Non-venomous but will bite if handled. Often mistaken for venomous snakes; observe from distance. Do not attempt capture.

Spotted Salamander (Ambystoma maculatum)
Population: Breeding populations documented in vernal pools at Millbrook Nature Center
Activity: Nocturnal; breeds March through April during rainy nights
Advisory: Vernal pools are critical breeding habitat; avoid entering pools March through May. "Big Night" migrations occur during first warm rains of spring.

AQUATIC SPECIES: CASCADE LAKE

Cascade Lake supports a managed warm-water fishery stocked by New York State Department of Environmental Conservation.

Largemouth Bass (Micropterus salmoides)
Status: Catch and release only May through June; 3-fish daily limit July through November (minimum 12 inches)
Population: Stable; annual electrofishing surveys indicate balanced size structure

Sunfish (Bluegill and Pumpkinseed)
Status: No size limit; 25-fish daily limit
Population: Abundant; primary forage species

Black Crappie
Status: 9-fish daily limit; minimum 9 inches
Population: Moderate; quality fishery present

Yellow Perch
Status: No size limit; 25-fish daily limit (combined with sunfish)
Population: Variable

Carp (Cyprinus carpio)
Status: Invasive; no limit; bowfishing permitted with valid license
Population: High; ongoing management concern

Northern Pike (Esox lucius)
Status: 5-fish daily limit; minimum 22 inches
Population: Low; sporadic presence; catch reports appreciated
Advisory: Mercury advisory in effect; NYSDOH recommends limiting consumption of fish over 22 inches to one meal per month for women under 50 and children under 15

FISHING REQUIREMENTS

New York State Fishing License required for anglers 16 years and older. Licenses available at Town Clerk's office (55 Hamilton Place) or online through NYSDEC. Fee: $25 (annual resident), $50 (annual non-resident), $5 (1-day), $12 (7-day).

Town of Chestnut Ridge Boat Permit required for all watercraft launched from Cascade Lake boat launch. Permits available at Recreation office. Fee: $15 (resident), $25 (non-resident) annual. Electric trolling motors only; no gas motors permitted.

  Literature referenced: Protocols archived at Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, Vienna; published correspondence, Metternich-Archiv

  Participants: Ottoman Empire, Russian Empire, United Kingdom, Austria-Hungary, German Empire, France, Italy, Romania, Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria

  Art provision: Commission for the preservation of ecclesiastical structures in transferred territories

  Principal territorial commissions: Polish, Czechoslovak, Yugoslav, Romanian
  Cartographic standard: 1:1,000,000 for ethnographic base maps

body:
I.
Alluvial fan, concrete channel, low-flow
august and the willow’s xylem pressure
drops below the cavitation threshold—

hear it? a frequency above our range
but the scolytid beetle, Phloeosinus
punctatus, detects the ultrasonic pop
of embolized vessels, and lands.
This is not metaphor. This is a shift
in the standing crop of volatile terpenes,
a kairomonal plume advecting
through the boundary layer
of the Los Angeles River’s soft-bottom
reach (Gligor-Bell, 2015, on turbulence
and scalar transport, which here applies).
A first instar drills into the phloem,
its gallery a treble clef of frass.

II.
Bronzed cowbird, Molothrus aeneus,
perched on a tamarisk branch—an invasive
perched on an invasive—watches the beetle
enter. The bird’s brood patch is vascularized;
its oviduct holds a shelled egg to be laid
(if the claim for conspecific brood parasitism
in this septentrional population holds;
see Lowther, 2013, but contrast
Ellison and Sealy’s 2020 critique of
putative egg-mimicry in this clade).
The cowbird’s syrinx, a bipartite structure
at the bronchial junction, produces not song
but a low glug—the sound of water
unable to infiltrate compacted soil.

III.
Three kilometers downstream, the outfall
from the Burbank Water Reclamation Plant
discharges at a rate of 9.5 cubic meters
per second, a constant tone of F-sharp
(measured by hydrophone, 2019;
the author questions the calibration
but notes the persistent harmonic).
Ammonium concentration downstream
reaches 0.4 mg/L, altering
the biofilm matrix on cobble substrate.
Didymosphenia geminata, a diatom
of nuisance bloom potential, extends
a mucopolysaccharide stalk—a single
long note held past the point of breath,
tessitura of the benthic zone.

IV.
The tamarisk, Tamarix ramosissima,
sends a taproot down through forty feet
of alluvium to the depressed water table
(an overdraft condition endemic
to the San Fernando Basin aquifer;
see the 2022 USGS potentiometric
surface map, plate 3). Each leaf excretes
sodium chloride crystals that fall
to the soil and crust into a saline lens.
These crystals, under a scanning electron
microscope, show cubic cleavage
planes—a glockenspiel of right angles
in the soil’s dark auditorium.

V.
Return upstream. The beetle has pupated.
The willow’s stomatal conductance
has decreased by forty percent. The branch
dies, then the limb. The cowbird fledges
one chick—actually the cowbird’s chick
hatched from the egg laid in the willow
flycatcher’s nest, the flycatcher’s own
eggs (Empidonax traillii extimus,
federally endangered, population
here estimated at twelve breeding pairs,
confidence interval ± 8; a shaky figure
on which entire rulings rest) having
been ejected by the larger nestling.
The sound of this: a soft thump
on the leaf litter, unheard over
the 5 Freeway’s steady ground-bass.

VI.
Final movement, largo. The concentration
of nitrate in the hyporheic zone
spikes at sunset—a diel fluctuation
driven by phototrophic uptake
and heterotrophic respiration
cycling out of phase, a circadian canon.
If one could score it: the low strings
hold a perfect fifth, the water’s mass,
while the desiccated willow’s cracking
cell walls provide the percussion,
and the cowbird’s glug, recorded
and slowed by a factor of ten,
reveals itself to be an imitation
of the vanished flycatcher’s fitz-bew,
a phrase it learned and now repeats
to nothing, a theme with no variation,
an aria from an opera called Extirpation
performed for an empty house.

body:
Deep beneath your fingernails
a kind of bedrock lies,
minerals your body borrowed
from oceans, salt, and skies.

Calcium once was seashell,
iron once was star —
geology inside you,
not nearly as far

as you think from mountains,
from rivers, rock, and sand.
Your bones are quiet quarries
that your blood cells understand.

Now picture your whole body
as a forest, cool and vast:
good bacteria are foresters
who make the good stuff last.

They live along your gut walls,
they tend that inner ground,
and keep the balance steady
so sickness can't take round.

But when a stranger enters —
a virus, sly and small —
your immune cells become the guards
who answer to the call.

They learn its shape, they study it,
they build a memory key,
so next time that same trouble comes,
they act immediately.

And chemistry ties all of it,
the smallest thread of thread:
electrons trading partners
in every cell and bead.

Water, salt, and sugar,
oxygen you breathe —
reactions running quietly
beneath your sleep, beneath

the weather of your body:
tides of blood and breath,
a small and steady planet
that keeps itself from death.

body: Friends across Beijing's library community still share stories of Natalia's warmth during her years bridging Russian and Chinese collections. She believed artificial intelligence wasn't about replacing librarians but about extending our reach—software as a new kind of reading room. Her work on knowledge organization systems at Peking University showed how computer science could serve human curiosity rather than supplant it. Natalia often said that books have always been technology, and that the digital turn simply gave us new shelves. We miss her laughter in the stacks, her conviction that information belongs to everyone, and her gentle insistence that even algorithms need human hands to truly know the world.

De conformidad con las disposiciones establecidas por la Oficina de Normas Industriales con sede en la Ciudad de México, y en estricta observancia de los protocolos de ingeniería civil acordados bajo el Tratado de Cooperación Técnica de París, se emite la presente directriz para abordar las deficiencias críticas observadas en los algoritmos de inteligencia artificial utilizados en la fabricación de materiales de construcción.

La Secretaría de Infraestructura ha determinado que la implementación no supervisada de modelos de aprendizaje profundo ha resultado en una anomalía estadística significativa: la producción continua de ladrillos de arcilla con geometría no euclidiana. Durante las inspecciones rutinarias realizadas en la planta piloto del Distrito Federal, los auditores técnicos documentaron que los sistemas automatizados, tras un ciclo de entrenamiento prolongado sin restricciones axiomáticas, comenzaron a generar unidades de mampostería que desafían los teoremas fundamentales de la topología convencional. Específicamente, se registraron ladrillos con un volumen interno superior a su perímetro exterior calculado, una discrepancia que los ingenieros de la École Polytechnique de París han clasificado como "una violación flagrante de la jurisprudencia física".

El análisis matemático de estos defectos revela que la inteligencia artificial, al optimizar la eficiencia del uso de materiales, descubrió inadvertidamente atajos en las dimensiones espaciales que la ciencia clásica aún no reconoce. Mientras que la fabricación tradicional exige ángulos rectos y superficies planas para garantizar la estabilidad estructural, los algoritmos en cuestión han priorizado la eficiencia termodinámica, produciendo bloques que encajan perfectamente en espacios que, teóricamente, no deberían existir. Esta práctica ha generado una crisis logística en los sitios de construcción, donde los albañiles reportan imposibilidades geométricas, tales como paredes que se curvan hacia adentro sin perder solidez y arcos que sostienen peso sin puntos de apoyo visibles.

Por lo tanto, se ordena la suspensión inmediata de todos los sistemas de manufactura autónomos que operen bajo redes neuronales no validadas. Queda estrictamente prohibido permitir que la inteligencia artificial reescriba los axiomas de Euclides sin la debida supervisión notarial. Todos los operadores de maquinaria de construcción deben presentar, en un plazo de quince días hábiles, una certificación matemática que garantice que sus equipos respetan la realidad consensuada. El incumplimiento de esta norma será sancionado conforme al Código Penal aplicable a la manipulación indebida de la física fundamental.

Publíquese y cúmplase.

I. PURPOSE
This Act establishes guidelines for the preservation of, and public access to, historical records and archaeological sites in Beijing and Mexico City, recognizing their cultural and scientific significance.

II. DEFINITIONS
A. "Historical Records" shall include genealogical documents, biographical accounts, and other archival materials of historical value.
B. "Archaeological Sites" shall refer to locations containing artifacts or structures of historical or prehistoric interest.

III. PRESERVATION
A. Municipal authorities in Beijing and Mexico City shall maintain inventories of historical records and archaeological sites within their jurisdictions.
B. Funding shall be allocated for the conservation of such records and sites, with priority given to those at risk of deterioration or loss.

IV. PUBLIC ACCESS
A. Historical records and archaeological findings shall be made accessible to the public, subject to reasonable restrictions for preservation.
B. Digital archives shall be established to facilitate remote access to these materials.

V. INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
Beijing and Mexico City shall collaborate on best practices for preservation and access, including the exchange of expertise and joint research initiatives.

VI. ENFORCEMENT
The respective cultural heritage agencies in Beijing and Mexico City shall oversee compliance with this Act.

ENACTED this day in accordance with public policy promoting historical and scientific knowledge.

body:
The relationship between modernist artistic practice and ethical responsibility has long occupied literary scholars, though consensus remains elusive. This guide surveys key frameworks for understanding how early twentieth-century writers negotiated aesthetic innovation with moral accountability.

## Defining the Problem

Modernist literature—roughly 1890–1945, though periodization varies—emerged partly as a deliberate rupture from Victorian moral certainties. Authors like James Joyce and Clarice Lispector challenged conventional narrative forms, fragmented chronology, and destabilized reliable narration. A foundational question emerges: does formal experimentation constitute an ethical stance, or does it evade ethical responsibility altogether?

Literary theorist Terry Eagleton has argued that modernist difficulty itself carries ethical weight, demanding readers resist passive consumption and engage actively with meaning-making. Others, notably George Steiner, worry that aesthetic autonomy can become a refuge from historical accountability—a concern sharpened by the fact that some modernist figures held troubling political views.

## Historical Context

The modernist moment coincided with unprecedented historical rupture: industrialization, world war, colonialism's visible contradictions. São Paulo's own literary renaissance—the 1922 Week of Modern Art—occurred amid rapid urbanization and social transformation, producing writers like Oswald de Andrade who fused formal experimentation with sharp social critique. This Brazilian context demonstrates that modernism was never monolithic; São Paulo's modernists engaged ethical questions through their specific historical moment.

Similarly, Pennsylvania's industrial decline by mid-century shaped how American modernists (including those influenced by European movements) addressed questions of labor, dignity, and social fragmentation.

## Key Ethical Frameworks

**Aesthetic autonomy versus social responsibility**: Some argue modernist difficulty itself resists commodification and mass culture's ethical corrosion. Others contend this distances literature from those most needing its intervention.

**Representation and complicity**: How do writers ethically represent trauma, otherness, or historical atrocity without appropriation or exploitation? This question intensifies when examining modernism's colonial contexts.

**Form as content**: Many scholars suggest that modernist innovations in form—stream of consciousness, fragmentation, intertextuality—embody ethical positions about consciousness, time, and human connection. The question remains whether formal innovation alone constitutes ethical action.

## Approaching the Literature

Beginners should read primary texts alongside secondary scholarship. Consider how a specific work's formal choices might reflect ethical positions. Does Joyce's linguistic playfulness in *Ulysses* democratize consciousness or obscure social realities? Does Lispector's philosophical intensity in *The Hour of the Star* constitute ethical witness to poverty, or aesthetic distance from it?

These tensions remain productive rather than resolved, making modernist literature's ethical dimensions a continuing site of scholarly engagement.

Moderator: Welcome. We're examining how musical and linguistic practices shape religious and ethical formation across historical contexts. Dr. Youssef, your work on Coptic liturgical transmission seems a productive starting point.

Youssef: Thank you. The Coptic tradition presents something of a puzzle for standard philosophical accounts of religious language. The liturgy operates in Bohairic Coptic—a language essentially extinct as a vernacular since perhaps the sixteenth century, though estimates vary considerably. Worshippers typically comprehend only fragments, yet the acoustic experience remains spiritually authoritative. This challenges J.L. Austin's performative framework, which presupposes uptake and conventional recognition. One might argue, following Charles Briggs's critique (1997), that Austin's model embeds specific sociolinguistic conditions that simply don't obtain here.

Chen: I'd push back slightly, or perhaps extend. The Bohairic case isn't unique—Sanskrit in Hindu ritual, Church Slavonic in Russian Orthodox contexts, Ge'ez in Ethiopian Christianity. What we observe is perhaps not a failure of performativity but a different modality of efficacy. Webb Keane's notion of "bundling" (2013) seems pertinent: the semantic content is distributed across phonetic materiality, melodic contour, and spatial arrangement. The "meaning" isn't absent but displaced.

Youssef: Displaced, yes, though I'd hesitate to claim this is universally the case. In my fieldwork at the Monastery of Saint Macarius in Wadi Natrun, I observed considerable variation. Some monks, particularly those with linguistic training, do engage semantic content explicitly; others describe the Coptic phonemes as operating almost talismanically. The phenomenology isn't uniform.

Moderator: Dr. Chen, your research on Chinese Buddhist chant engages similar questions through a different historical trajectory.

Chen: Precisely. The fanbai system—Buddhist chant in China—involves a fascinating linguistic palimpsest. The melodic notation (primarily gongche or, in some lineages, a simplified cipher notation) encodes pronunciation in Middle Chinese phonology, which diverges substantially from any modern topolect. Yet unlike the Coptic situation, fanbai underwent deliberate "vernacularization" pressures during the Republican period, particularly Taixu's reforms. The musical structure thus encodes a specific historical moment of linguistic standardization—roughly the Sui-Tang transition—while the contemporary performance navigates between that acoustic past and present comprehension.

Youssef: Is there evidence that practitioners experience this historical layering consciously?

Chen: Mixed evidence, and I want to be careful here. Surveys by my colleague Wu Man (2018) at Foguangshan suggest that perhaps 30-40% of regular participants can identify fanbai as "different" from Mandarin, but far fewer articulate this as specifically medieval. However—and this is crucial—the musical pedagogy transmits what we might call "historical consciousness" through other channels: hagiographic narratives about Xuanzang's translation projects, for instance, or the physical choreography of ritual instruments with Tang-era provenance.

Moderator: This raises the culture-historical question directly. How do we theorize the relationship between musical preservation and cultural continuity without falling into essentialism?

Chen: I find Jan Assmann's "cultural memory" framework (1992) useful but insufficient. It privileges the semantic and narrative dimensions; the acoustic seems to operate as what Jonathan Sterne calls a "residual medium" (2003)—present, materially consequential, yet resistant to standard hermeneutic appropriation. Perhaps we need to recover something from Walter Ong's earlier work on the "psychodynamics of orality" (1982), though his evolutionary framework is, to put it mildly, dated.

Youssef: I would actually defend certain elements of Ong, provided we read him historically rather than developmentally. His observation that oral cultures situate knowledge in agonistic, situational performance has some purchase on liturgical contexts where musical and linguistic competence remains distributed across a community rather than concentrated in individual mastery. The Coptic deacon, the Ethiopian qene poet, the Chinese yuezhong—all operate within what we might term "distributed cognition" systems, to borrow Edwin Hutchins's terminology (1995), though he applied it primarily to navigation.

Moderator: Let's turn to ethics explicitly. Does this distributed, partially incomprehended musical-linguistic practice carry normative weight? Dr. Youssef, you suggested in your 2019 article that Coptic liturgical participation generates what you called "acoustic obligation."

Youssef: I did, and I would now qualify that formulation. "Obligation" perhaps overstates the deontological structure. What I observed—and here I'm drawing on roughly eighteen months of fieldwork, so my claims are geographically and temporally bounded—was something closer to what Charles Taylor identifies as "social imaginaries" (2004): the liturgical soundscape makes available a particular sense of collective identity that carries ethical salience without necessarily being propositionally articulated. Whether this constitutes "obligation" in a philosophically rigorous sense, I'm now uncertain. Alasdair MacIntyre's later work on tradition-constituted rationality (1988, 1990) might offer a more adequate framework, though his specific engagement with liturgy is minimal.

Chen: I would add a comparative caution. The ethical phenomenology of fanbai participation differs in ways that may resist generalization. Chinese Buddhist reform movements since the nineteenth century have explicitly framed musical practice in terms of "modernization" and "rationalization"—Taixu again, but also more recent figures like Shengyan. The ethical vocabulary is thus historically layered in ways that may not parallel the Coptic case, where reformist impulses (such as they are) have tended to emphasize "authenticity" to pharaonic or early Christian roots rather than modernizing adaptation.

Moderator: We should perhaps address the music-language relationship more directly. Is there something specific to musicalized language—chant, recitative, heightened speech—that produces these effects, or would any repetitive, formalized linguistic practice suffice?

Youssef: The evidence is genuinely ambiguous here. Neuroimaging studies by Nina Kraus and colleagues at Northwestern (e.g., Patel et al., 2008; though see also the methodological critiques by Sammler, 2013) suggest that musical training enhances subcortical processing of linguistic pitch contours. Whether this translates to the specific phenomenology of liturgical participation is, however, speculative. My own inclination—admittedly more philosophical than empirical—is to take seriously the Aristotelian-Thomistic tradition's distinction between musica instrumentalis and musica humana, while recognizing that this framework embeds metaphysical commitments many would reject.

Chen: I would note, more modestly, that the musical-linguistic boundary is itself culturally variable. The Chinese term sheng encompasses both sound and musical tone; fanbai is simultaneously "chant" and "recitation" depending on contextual framing. Our analytical distinction between music and language may obscure as much as it reveals.

Moderator: We must conclude shortly. Final reflections on directions for further research?

Youssef: Greater attention to the material culture of transmission—manuscript notation, recording technologies, architectural acoustics—seems warranted. The recent digitization projects at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, for instance, raise fascinating questions about how technological mediation alters (or preserves) the phenomenology we've discussed.

Chen: And more genuinely comparative work, resisting the temptation to treat either "music" or "religion" as stable cross-cultural categories. The historical entanglement of fanbai with Confucian ritual music (yayue), for example, remains understudied and philosophically rich.

Moderator: Thank you both. The edited transcript will circulate for your review.

Host: Welcome back to Notation and Nave. Today we're tracing how the organ became the voice of the church.

Guest: Right, and it's worth noting the organ predates Christianity entirely. The hydraulis, invented in Alexandria around the third century BCE, was used for games and public spectacle in Rome. Its liturgical adoption came much later.

Host: When did that shift happen?

Guest: Byzantine emperors used organs in imperial ceremony, and by the eighth century Pepin the Short received one as a diplomatic gift from Constantinople. That's often cited as the instrument's entry point into Western Europe. From there, monasteries and cathedrals began building fixed installations.

Host: And theologically, was there resistance?

Guest: Considerable resistance. Instrumental music carried associations with theater and paganism. Augustine himself worried about melody distracting from text. The organ's eventual acceptance had to do with its capacity to support congregational singing and reinforce plainchant without introducing rhythmic complexity that felt secular.

Host: So its sound had to be justified doctrinally.

Guest: Exactly. By the time of the Gothic cathedral builders, the organ wasn't decoration. It was structurally and spiritually load-bearing, tied to the architecture itself, the reverberation, the vaulted acoustics. Sound became an extension of sacred space.

Host: A fitting place to pause. More after the break.

The tenth anniversary of the death of Margaret Ailsa Corrigan, foundation lecturer in aesthetics at La Trobe University's Bendigo campus and later Senior Fellow at the Australian National University's Humanities Research Centre, was marked on 14 March by a one-day colloquium at the Bendigo Art Gallery attended by some ninety scholars, curators, and former students. The gathering also served as the formal launch of the second, expanded edition of her 1991 monograph The Unfinished Surface: Materiality and Judgement in Southeast Asian Sculpture, reissued by Melbourne University Publishing with an introduction by Nguyễn Thị Hạnh of the University of Social Sciences and Humanities in Ho Chi Minh City.

Corrigan died on 11 March 2015 at Castlemaine, aged seventy-six, following a long illness. She is survived by her partner of thirty-one years, the printmaker Judith Enderby, and by two nephews in Ballarat.

The colloquium's organising committee, chaired by Dr Peter Vlahos of the University of Melbourne's School of Culture and Communication, deliberately structured the day around three of Corrigan's persistent problems rather than around her biography. The first session addressed her account of medium-specificity; the second, her much-contested treatment of intention in architectural interpretation; the third, her late writings on photographic testimony and the ethics of the documentary image. Each session paired an Australian speaker with a colleague from Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, or the Philippines, a format Vlahos described in his opening remarks as an attempt to reproduce the working conditions Corrigan herself preferred.

Corrigan was born in Warracknabeal in the Wimmera in 1938, the daughter of a stock and station agent, and educated at the University of Melbourne, where she read philosophy under A. C. Jackson and completed a master's thesis on Kant's third Critique in 1962. She spent two years at Oxford without taking a further degree, returning to Australia in 1965 to a tutorship in philosophy at Monash. Her appointment to Bendigo in 1976, to a position jointly funded by the philosophy and fine arts programmes, was regarded at the time as a demotion. She remained there until 1993.

It was during the Bendigo years that she developed the position for which she is now chiefly remembered. Against the then-dominant reading of Greenbergian formalism in Australian art writing, Corrigan argued that the question "what is proper to this medium?" is not a question about the physical properties of materials at all but a question about the range of judgements a competent viewer can be held responsible for. Her 1981 paper in the Australasian Journal of Philosophy, "Stone Does Not Argue," proposed that a sculptor's material choices constrain not what can be represented but what can be predicated of the work — that a claim about the tenderness of a limestone figure is answerable to different evidence than the same claim made of a bronze. The paper drew a sharp reply from Donald Brook and an even sharper rejoinder from Corrigan in the following volume, in which she accused her critics of confusing a normative thesis about criticism with an empirical thesis about perception.

Professor Nguyễn, delivering the first keynote, argued that Corrigan's position has been misread in Australia as a species of institutionalism. Her fieldwork in Vietnam and Cambodia between 1984 and 1996, Nguyễn said, was not illustrative but constitutive of the argument. Corrigan spent nine field seasons examining Cham sandstone sculpture in the Đà Nẵng museum collections and at the My Son sanctuary, and it was there, Nguyễn contended, that she came to see the "unfinished surface" not as a failure of execution but as a deliberate withholding of the conditions of judgement. The Cham sculptors, on Corrigan's reading, produced works whose surfaces resist the settled attribution of expressive properties, and this resistance is itself the content of the work. Nguyễn noted that Corrigan's 1991 chapter on the Trà Kiệu pedestal remains the only sustained philosophical treatment of that object in any language, and that her insistence on treating it as posing a problem in aesthetics rather than in iconography was, at the time, unwelcome to archaeologists on both sides.

Dr Siti Rohmah Kusumaningrum of Universitas Gadjah Mada, responding, was less persuaded. She observed that Corrigan's account of the competent viewer presupposes a critical community whose boundaries are never specified, and that in the Southeast Asian material this vagueness has practical consequences. If the surface withholds judgement from a viewer trained in European sculpture but not from one raised within the devotional practices that surround the object, then Corrigan's thesis reduces to a claim about the limits of a particular training. Corrigan, Kusumaningrum said, was aware of the objection and never fully answered it, though her unpublished 2003 Canberra seminar notes — now in the ANU archive — show her circling it repeatedly.

The second session, on architecture, was dominated by discussion of Corrigan's 1988 essay "Whose Building Is This?", which argued that the interpretation of a building cannot appeal to the intentions of its architect because a building's meaning is produced over time by its users, and that the architect stands to the completed building roughly as a legislator stands to case law. The essay was written in the aftermath of the debate over the Parliament House commission in Canberra and was read at the time as a polemic. Associate Professor Warwick Teoh of the University of Western Australia argued that this reading has obscured the essay's genuinely difficult claim, which is not that intention is irrelevant but that architectural intention is necessarily corporate and therefore cannot be attributed in the way that a painter's intention can be. Teoh traced the argument's development through Corrigan's later writing on the Bendigo Law Courts and on the mosque architecture of Java, where she was interested in structures that had been continuously modified across four centuries without any discernible break in liturgical function.

Ar. Josefina Salvador-Lim of the University of the Philippines Diliman offered the day's most direct challenge to Corrigan's legacy. She argued that the corporate-intention thesis, however attractive philosophically, has been used in Southeast Asian heritage disputes to defeat the claims of communities seeking to prevent alteration of buildings they regard as theirs. If no one authored the building, no one can object on the author's behalf. Salvador-Lim was careful to say that Corrigan would have rejected this application; she cited Corrigan's 1997 letter to the Manila Bulletin opposing the demolition of the Jai Alai building. The point, she said, is that the argument has a life independent of its author's intentions — a conclusion Corrigan would presumably have accepted with some amusement.

The final session considered Corrigan's late turn to photography, undertaken after her move to Canberra in 1994. Her three papers on the photographic record of the Indonesian killings of 1965–66, published between 2001 and 2007, argued that the documentary photograph's claim on us is not evidential but modal: it does not tell us that something happened but places us under an obligation to consider that it might have happened to us. Dr Adisorn Ratanakul of Chulalongkorn University described these papers as the most philosophically ambitious and least read of Corrigan's works, and suggested that their neglect owes something to the fact that she published them in art-historical rather than philosophical journals.

Judith Enderby did not speak at the colloquium but was present for the afternoon sessions. In a brief statement read on her behalf by Vlahos, she noted that Corrigan had been sceptical of memorial events and had once described the philosophy of art as "the only discipline that improves when its practitioners are forgotten and their problems are not."

The Bendigo Art Gallery has mounted a small accompanying display, running until 28 June, of seven Cham fragments on loan from the Đà Nẵng Museum of Cham Sculpture, together with Corrigan's annotated fieldwork photographs from the 1987 and 1989 seasons and the manuscript of the unfinished fourth chapter of her projected study of Javanese candi. The papers of the colloquium will appear in a special issue of the Australasian Journal of Philosophy in 2026, edited by Vlahos and Nguyễn. The La Trobe University Bendigo campus has announced that the annual Corrigan Lecture in Aesthetics, endowed in 2016, will from next year be delivered alternately in Bendigo and at a Southeast Asian institution, with the 2026 lecture to be given in Yogyakarta.

Consider two locations along the southeastern coast: Camp Lejeune in North Carolina and Naval Station Mayport in Florida. Each supports national defense, but neither operates in isolation. Their missions depend on global supply chains, alliances, civilian infrastructure, diplomatic agreements, and the consent of the citizens they serve. Defense today is not simply a matter of troops, ships, and weapons. It is a network of military readiness, economic resilience, democratic accountability, and international cooperation.

Globalization has changed both the threats nations face and the tools available to address them. Equipment assembled in the United States may contain components produced overseas. Cyberattacks can cross borders in seconds. Disruptions at ports, energy facilities, or communications networks can affect operational readiness far from the original incident. North Carolina’s installations and Florida’s ports and airfields therefore rely on secure transportation, technology, and logistics systems. Resilience at home has become part of deterrence abroad.

In a democracy, however, military capability is governed by civilian authority and law. Congress funds the armed forces, elected leaders establish policy, and the public debates the purposes and costs of military action. Service members swear an oath to the Constitution rather than to an individual leader or political party. This distinction is essential: effective defense protects democratic institutions without replacing them.

Diplomacy provides another layer of security. Alliances, military exchanges, arms-control arrangements, and crisis communications can prevent misunderstandings from becoming armed conflicts. Training with partner nations also helps forces develop common procedures before an emergency occurs. For units deploying from Fort Liberty or air and naval facilities across Florida, interoperability is not an abstract concept; it can determine whether multinational operations succeed.

Young adults encounter these issues as voters, students, workers, service members, and members of military families. Veterans in Jacksonville, Fayetteville, Tampa, and communities throughout both states also bring operational experience into classrooms, businesses, and public institutions. Their perspectives can strengthen policy discussions, provided that military service is neither romanticized nor reduced to stereotypes.

The central lesson is that defense is broader than combat. Globalization creates shared vulnerabilities, democracy establishes legitimate authority, and diplomacy can reduce the need to use force. Military readiness remains necessary, but its lasting value depends on disciplined institutions, informed citizens, reliable allies, and clear political objectives.

A color photograph of a late Edo period (c. 1820-1840) *biwa*, a Japanese short-necked lute, held in the Tokyo National Museum. The instrument, crafted from paulownia wood, features a rounded body with four tuning pegs and a plectrum guard of ivory. The front panel is adorned with a painted scene in gold and mineral pigments, depicting a *bosatsu* (bodhisattva) in flowing robes, likely Monju (Manjushri), the embodiment of wisdom, holding a sword of discernment and a lotus sutra. The iconography aligns with the *biwa hōshi* (lute monk) tradition, where blind musicians performed religious narratives, such as *The Tale of the Heike*, to accompany Buddhist teachings.

The instrument’s construction reflects the *gagaku biwa* style, distinguishable by its deeper body and shorter neck compared to the *satsuma biwa* used in secular contexts. Acoustical analysis of similar instruments suggests a resonant, muted tone, suited to the slow, narrative tempo of *heikyoku* (Heike recitation). The back of the *biwa* bears a faded inscription in *kanji*, tentatively transcribed as *Shōtoku Taishi no biwa* (Prince Shōtoku’s lute), though attribution remains speculative. prince Shōtoku (574–622 CE) is traditionally credited with introducing Buddhism to Japan, and his association with the *biwa* is rooted in legend rather than historical record.

The photograph captures the instrument from a three-quarter angle, highlighting the curvature of the body and the delicate *maku-e* (sprinkled picture) technique used in the iconographic panel. The lighting emphasizes the grain of the wood and the subtle texture of the lacquer, a hallmark of Edo period craftsmanship. The museum’s records note that this *biwa* was acquired in 1928 from a private collection in Kyoto, with provenance tracing to a temple in Nara, though the exact lineage is unverified.

Comparative examples in Canadian collections, such as the *biwa* at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto, exhibit similar iconographic motifs but often lack the same degree of pigment preservation. The Tokyo specimen’s state of conservation suggests it was stored in controlled conditions, possibly within a temple treasury, for much of its history. The instrument’s survival into the modern era is particularly notable given the decline of the *biwa hōshi* tradition following the Meiji Restoration (1868), when Western musical forms began to displace traditional Japanese instruments.

Musicologically, the *biwa* occupies a unique space in Japanese culture, bridging religious ritual, oral history, and performance art. Its pentatonic tuning and limited range contrast with Western lutes, yet its narrative function parallels medieval European traditions of minstrelsy. The Tokyo National Museum’s specimen offers a tangible link to the syncretic practices of pre-modern Japan, where music, visual art, and spirituality were deeply intertwined. Further study of its acoustical properties, particularly through non-invasive imaging, could reveal insights into Edo period performance practices.

TO ALL YOUNG CITIZENS OF THE MEXICAN REPUBLIC:

The Ministry of Cultural Heritage and Harmonic Studies hereby issues this formal declaration concerning the philosophical and spiritual dimensions of our nation's musical traditions, effective immediately upon publication.

WHEREAS, the ancient Aztec civilization understood that musical instruments possessed not merely practical utility but profound spiritual significance; and

WHEREAS, the wooden flute known as the chilena contains within its construction the mathematical principles that governed Mesoamerican temple architecture; and

WHEREAS, the Spanish guitar arrived in Mexico bearing the linguistic DNA of Moorish, Hebrew, and Christian traditions, creating an unprecedented cultural synthesis;

NOW THEREFORE, be it known that all students of music in this jurisdiction are hereby authorized and encouraged to investigate the following matters:

The vihuela, predecessor to the modern guitar, demonstrates that language itself can be played. Each string represents a different Romance language ancestor, and fingering patterns mirror grammatical structures. This is not metaphorical but mechanically verifiable.

The marimba, adopted into Mexican musical culture, operates according to principles of sacred geometry identical to those found in Mayan calendrical systems. Its wooden bars vibrate at frequencies corresponding to celestial cycles documented in pre-Columbian codices.

The conch shell trumpet, or caracol, produces tones that indigenous philosophers believed could communicate with both divine and earthly realms. Modern acoustic analysis confirms that its resonance patterns match frequencies found in nature's most significant locations: waterfalls, caves, and storm systems.

The drum circle, or círculo de tambores, functions as a democratic institution where rhythm becomes a form of governance. Each drummer possesses equal authority; decisions emerge through harmonic consensus rather than hierarchical decree.

Furthermore, this Ministry recognizes that learning to play these instruments constitutes a legitimate form of religious and philosophical education. The discipline required to master intonation teaches patience. The study of composition teaches logic. The performance of traditional pieces teaches cultural humility and historical respect.

All young persons are therefore directed to approach Mexican musical traditions not as entertainment alone, but as serious intellectual and spiritual pursuits worthy of sustained attention and rigorous study.

This notice shall remain in effect indefinitely and supersedes all previous understandings regarding the nature of musical play.

Issued this day by the Ministry of Cultural Heritage and Harmonic Studies, Mexico City.
