AN ACT concerning the siting, design, construction, operation, repowering, and decommissioning of offshore wind energy facilities in the Great Lakes; establishing engineering, ecological, and monitoring requirements; providing for interagency review and enforcement; and prescribing penalties.

I. LEGISLATIVE FINDINGS AND PURPOSE

Section 1. The General Assembly finds all of the following:

(a) The Great Lakes constitute a connected freshwater system of exceptional ecological, hydrological, cultural, and economic significance, comprising Lakes Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario and their associated tributaries, wetlands, shorelands, benthic habitats, and airsheds.

(b) Utility-scale wind energy facilities proposed for deployment in the Great Lakes present engineering conditions materially different from those encountered by fixed-bottom facilities in the Atlantic Ocean or other marine environments, including seasonal ice formation, fetch-dependent wave climates, lakebed variability, seiches, storm-generated water-level fluctuations, freshwater corrosion regimes, and proximity to densely populated shorelines.

(c) The ecological effects of such facilities cannot be evaluated solely through project-level estimates of annual energy production or conventional terrestrial avian surveys. A technically adequate evaluation shall account for migratory pathways, nocturnal flight behavior, pelagic and benthic processes, fish spawning and nursery habitat, invasive species vectors, electromagnetic fields, acoustic emissions, navigation, and cumulative effects across the basin.

(d) The public interest requires that engineering design and ecological protection be treated as interdependent elements of facility approval, rather than as sequential or severable obligations.

The purposes of this Act are to:

(1) establish minimum standards for the investigation, design, installation, operation, and removal of offshore wind energy facilities;

(2) require scientifically defensible assessment of ecological and cumulative effects;

(3) preserve navigational safety, public access, fisheries, cultural resources, and the integrity of Great Lakes water and sediment systems; and

(4) ensure that facilities are financially and technically capable of complete decommissioning at the end of their useful service lives.

II. DEFINITIONS

Section 2. As used in this Act:

(a) “Applicant” means a person, utility, governmental entity, consortium, or other legal entity seeking approval for a facility.

(b) “Facility” means an offshore wind energy generating installation and all associated foundations, turbines, electrical collection systems, export cables, substations, meteorological equipment, service platforms, scour protection, anchors, moorings, access routes, and onshore interconnection works located below the ordinary high-water mark or functionally integrated therewith.

(c) “Great Lakes waterbed” means the unconsolidated sediment, bedrock, and biological substrate underlying the waters of any Great Lake under the jurisdiction of this State.

(d) “High-energy event” means a storm, seiche, ice-loading episode, vessel impact, or other event having a return period or design consequence specified by the applicable engineering standard adopted under Section 5.

(e) “Repowering” means replacement or material modification of turbines, foundations, electrical systems, or other principal components that extends or substantially alters the operating life, capacity, or loading regime of a facility.

(f) “Sensitive ecological receptor” means a species, habitat, process, or human use reasonably susceptible to material adverse effects from construction or operation, including fish spawning grounds, benthic communities, migratory birds, bat populations, wetlands, drinking-water intakes, commercial and subsistence fisheries, and designated cultural or protected areas.

(g) “Water-level datum” means a vertically referenced elevation system tied to an established Great Lakes datum and used consistently for bathymetric, structural, hydrodynamic, and construction calculations.

III. APPLICATION AND BASELINE INVESTIGATION

Section 3. An application shall not be deemed complete unless it contains:

(a) a geophysical and geotechnical investigation sufficient to characterize bathymetry, sediment stratigraphy, bedrock depth, shear strength, consolidation behavior, cyclic loading response, liquefaction potential, debris fields, and geohazards along every proposed foundation, cable, and anchor corridor;

(b) at least two years of baseline observations, or a scientifically justified equivalent approved by the Department of Environment, addressing wind, waves, currents, water levels, ice, suspended sediment, turbidity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, fish distribution, bird migration, bat activity, benthic assemblages, and existing underwater sound;

(c) a navigation and marine-traffic assessment identifying commercial shipping lanes, ferry routes, recreational boating corridors, fishing grounds, search-and-rescue operations, and designated anchorage or refuge areas;

(d) a cable burial and thermal-dissipation analysis accounting for sediment composition, burial depth, ampacity, magnetic-field exposure, potential cable exposure, thermal plume behavior, and interference with future waterbed uses; and

(e) a cumulative-effects assessment addressing existing and reasonably foreseeable facilities, transmission corridors, dredging, shoreline armoring, shipping, contaminants, invasive species, climate-driven water-level change, and other stressors affecting the same ecological receptors.

The Department may require additional baseline duration where interannual variability, ice conditions, migratory timing, or other site characteristics render the submitted record insufficient for reliable inference.

IV. ENGINEERING DESIGN REQUIREMENTS

Section 4. A facility shall be designed by a professional engineer licensed in this State and qualified by education and experience in offshore, marine, structural, geotechnical, or wind-energy engineering, as applicable. The design basis shall identify all governing limit states, load combinations, material factors, consequence classes, inspection intervals, and uncertainty treatments.

Section 5. The Department of Transportation, in consultation with the Department of Environment and the State Geological Survey, shall adopt rules requiring that facility design conform, to the extent applicable, with current editions of recognized standards including the International Electrotechnical Commission 61400 series, the American Bureau of Shipping Rules for Building and Classing Offshore Wind Turbine Installations, the American Society of Civil Engineers 7, the American Petroleum Institute Recommended Practice 2A or successor offshore foundation guidance, and applicable Great Lakes navigation and electrical-safety requirements.

Where a recognized standard does not address freshwater ice, lakebed conditions, or a site-specific failure mode, the applicant shall submit a qualified engineering basis demonstrating equivalent or greater reliability. Reliance upon an oceanic design standard without adjustment for freshwater ice accretion, ice-induced vibration, thermal cycling, or lakebed scour shall not satisfy this section.

Section 6. Foundations and support structures shall be proportioned for:

(a) extreme and fatigue wind loading, including wake effects and turbulence intensity;

(b) combined wind, wave, current, ice, seismic, hydrodynamic, and operational loading;

(c) ice crushing, buckling, ridging, rubble accumulation, and cyclic interaction at the waterline;

(d) differential settlement, lateral spreading, scour, erosion, and loss of embedment;

(e) vessel collision commensurate with local traffic and facility consequence class; and

(f) abnormal conditions, including loss of electrical control, emergency shutdown, blade throw, fire, flooding, and progressive failure.

The applicant shall demonstrate that the foundation and its connection to the waterbed remain stable under credible high-energy events and that any anticipated residual deformation does not compromise electrical isolation, navigational clearance, or ecological containment measures.

Section 7. The design shall minimize permanent alteration of the waterbed. Scour protection shall be selected on the basis of hydraulic performance, stability, constructability, long-term maintenance, and ecological compatibility. Materials shall be clean, durable, and free of contaminants, deleterious fines, and living organisms capable of introducing or propagating aquatic invasive species.

V. CONSTRUCTION CONTROLS

Section 8. Before commencement of in-water construction, the applicant shall submit a construction environmental control plan identifying equipment, work windows, pile-driving sequences, dredging quantities, sediment controls, spill response, vessel routes, noise attenuation, monitoring stations, and stop-work criteria.

Pile driving and other impulsive activities shall employ technically practicable attenuation measures, including bubble curtains, isolation sleeves, cofferdams, vibratory installation, or equivalent methods. The Department may prohibit impulsive construction during fish spawning, larval drift, peak migration, or other periods when measured or modeled exposure would cause injury, behavioral exclusion, or material habitat disruption.

Dredging, trenching, and cable installation shall be conducted to minimize resuspension and dispersal of contaminated or oxygen-demanding sediment. Spoil shall not be discharged into open water except pursuant to a specific permit supported by sediment chemistry, grain-size analysis, contaminant fate modeling, and a finding that no practicable upland or confined disposal alternative provides equivalent protection.

Section 9. Construction vessels, barges, anchors, and equipment shall comply with an aquatic invasive species prevention plan. Ballast-water exchange, hull fouling, equipment decontamination, bilge management, and transfer of residual sediment shall be documented. A vessel or item of equipment that has operated in an infested waterbody shall not enter the project area without treatment or inspection approved by the Department.

VI. ECOLOGICAL PERFORMANCE AND MONITORING

Section 10. The permittee shall implement a monitoring program sufficient to distinguish facility-related effects from natural variability and background trends. Monitoring shall include, as appropriate:

(a) vertical and horizontal distribution of migratory birds and bats, including nocturnal radar or equivalent remote-sensing observations;

(b) fish abundance, spawning activity, movement, and habitat use in the project area and reference areas;

(c) benthic community composition, substrate alteration, colonization of artificial structures, and changes in sediment oxygen demand;

(d) underwater sound during construction and operation, including frequency spectra and exposure at sensitive receptors;

(e) electromagnetic fields associated with inter-array and export cables; and

(f) changes in turbidity, temperature, currents, and sediment transport.

Protocols shall be established before construction, use quality assurance and quality control procedures, and provide for raw-data preservation, calibration records, metadata, statistical power analysis, and public release subject only to lawful protection of security-sensitive information.

Section 11. Artificial reef effects shall not be credited as ecological mitigation unless the permittee demonstrates, through site-specific evidence, that introduced hard substrate produces a net ecological benefit and does not facilitate invasive species, alter predator-prey relationships, concentrate fishing mortality, interfere with fish passage, or displace valued soft-bottom habitat.

The permittee shall not use avoidance of documented bird or bat mortality, fish injury, or benthic degradation as a basis for claiming mitigation credit for unrelated habitat enhancement.

VII. OPERATION, INSPECTION, AND ADAPTIVE MANAGEMENT

Section 12. Each facility shall maintain an operations and maintenance program addressing structural inspections, nondestructive testing, corrosion protection, blade and drivetrain condition, cable exposure, scour, ice damage, debris, emergency access, and electrical safety. Inspection intervals shall be shortened following a high-energy event or when monitoring identifies a changed failure probability.

The permittee shall notify the Department within twenty-four hours after a structural failure, cable exposure exceeding the approved tolerance, release of hydraulic fluid or other hazardous material, unplanned turbine collapse, vessel collision, or mortality event exceeding an approved threshold.

Section 13. The Department may require operational curtailment, seasonal shutdown, altered turbine start-up speeds, lighting modification, or other corrective action when monitoring demonstrates that a facility is causing material adverse effects to a sensitive ecological receptor. Such action shall be based on pre-established action thresholds where practicable and shall be reviewed using the best available scientific and engineering information.

VIII. DECOMMISSIONING AND FINANCIAL ASSURANCE

Section 14. Before construction, the applicant shall submit a decommissioning plan providing for removal of turbines, towers, substations, cables where removal is technically practicable and environmentally preferable, foundations to the approved depth, scour protection, debris, and temporary works.

The plan shall evaluate alternative end states, including complete removal, partial removal, and approved conversion of structures for habitat or research purposes. No structure may remain in place merely because removal is costly unless the Department finds that retention provides a demonstrated net environmental and navigational benefit and does not impair future waterbed use.

Section 15. The permittee shall maintain financial assurance sufficient to fund decommissioning, site restoration, monitoring, and post-removal corrective action. The amount shall be calculated using an independent engineer’s cost estimate, escalated for inflation and adjusted at least every five years or upon repowering. Financial assurance shall remain available notwithstanding insolvency, transfer, abandonment, or expiration of the operating permit.

IX. ENFORCEMENT

Section 16. A violation of this Act or a permit issued under it is subject to a civil penalty not exceeding fifty thousand dollars for each day of violation, in addition to restoration costs and any administrative order authorized by law. A person who knowingly submits materially false engineering data, monitoring results, or financial-assurance information is subject to suspension or revocation of the permit and referral for prosecution under applicable law.

A permit may be transferred only upon demonstration that the transferee possesses the technical competence, financial capacity, environmental records, and emergency-response capability necessary to comply with this Act.

Section 17. This Act shall be liberally construed to protect the ecological integrity and public uses of the Great Lakes while enabling reliable energy infrastructure whose design, construction, and operation satisfy applicable engineering and environmental performance requirements.

WHEREAS, the exigencies of global interconnectedness, hereinafter referred to as the Condition of Globalization, have rendered the traditional, insular mechanisms of public administration insufficient for the preservation of domestic tranquility and the common defense; and

WHEREAS, the administrative state of North Carolina, in its sovereign capacity, has identified a critical nexus between the fluidity of international commerce, the transnational movement of persons, and the proliferation of seditious doctrines that threaten the foundational principles of republican governance; and

WHEREAS, the security of the State is no longer a function confined to the physical repulsion of armed invasion but extends to the integrity of its administrative apparatus against the corrosive influence of external authoritarian models, particularly those refined in the Germanic principalities under the doctrine of *Polizeiwissenschaft*, which seek to subordinate individual liberty to the absolute administrative efficiency of the state; and

WHEREAS, the Governor, acting under the plenary authority vested by the Constitution of North Carolina to execute the laws and preserve the State from insurrection and administrative subversion, deems it necessary to erect a specialized organ dedicated to the prophylactic management of these composite threats;

NOW, THEREFORE, I, ABSALOM J. CARTER, Governor of the State of North Carolina, by virtue of the authority in me vested, do hereby order and decree as follows:

I. ESTABLISHMENT AND DESIGNATION
There is hereby established within the Executive Department, an administrative agency to be known as the Bureau of Trans-Atlantic Administrative Security Coordination, hereinafter the “Bureau.” The Bureau shall be a cabinet-level agency, its Director reporting directly to the Governor and the Council of State.

II. MISSION AND DOCTRINAL PURVIEW
The Bureau’s paramount mission is the neutralization of systemic administrative vulnerabilities generated by the Condition of Globalization. It shall operate on the doctrinal principle that public administration is the primary terrain of twenty-first-century conflict, wherein hostile entities, whether foreign states or non-state networks, exploit the procedural pathways of open societies to implant authoritarian praxis. The Bureau’s specific purview encompasses:
A. The monitoring and analysis of international public law and comparative administrative procedure, with a specific focus on the federated states of Germany, to identify and catalog mechanisms of social control, population registration, and executive preemption that could be adapted for domestic application by hostile actors.
B. The conduct of security audits of all State agencies whose statutory remit involves cross-border flows, including but not limited to the Department of Commerce, the State Ports Authority, and the University of North Carolina system’s international exchange programs, to assess their susceptibility to administrative penetration.
C. The development of counter-administrative protocols designed to inoculate State procedures against the importation of illiberal governance techniques, ensuring that the administrative necessity never eclipses constitutional due process.

III. ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE
The Bureau shall be organized into three primary divisions, reflecting the tripartite nature of its security mission:
A. The Division of Systemic Cartography. This division shall engage in the continuous mapping of global administrative genealogies. It shall maintain a classified registry, to be known as the Index of Transmissible Administrative Pathologies, cataloging specific statutes, regulations, and judicial doctrines from foreign jurisdictions, with a detailed focus on the post-1945 German administrative court system, that represent vectors for authoritarian creep. A special subsection, the Hanover Desk, shall be dedicated to the real-time translation and jurisprudential analysis of rulings from the German Federal Administrative Court (*Bundesverwaltungsgericht*) that pertain to the police power and the limitation of fundamental rights for reasons of state security.
B. The Division of Procedural Fortification. This division shall serve as an internal consultancy to all North Carolina executive agencies. Its agents shall embed within routine bureaucratic processes—licensing, procurement, public health reporting—to identify and reseal procedural gaps. The division is authorized to issue Administrative Security Directives (ASDs) that mandate specific alterations to agency workflow, record-keeping, and inter-agency data sharing. An ASD carries the force of executive order and may only be appealed to the Governor in camera.
C. The Division of Trans-Atlantic Liaison and Extraction. Recognizing that the most effective defense requires an understanding of the offensive architecture, this division is authorized to establish a covert presence within the administrative apparatus of targeted German states, specifically Lower Saxony and Baden-Württemberg. Operating under non-official cover, agents shall seek to extract administrative intelligence regarding the operationalization of the *Verfassungsschutz* (Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution) surveillance methodologies as applied to municipal administration. This intelligence shall be repurposed to harden North Carolina’s own municipal and county administrative structures against similar surveillance modalities, should they be deployed by domestic adversaries.

IV. THE DOCTRINE OF ADMINISTRATIVE PREEMPTION
The Bureau is guided by the principle that the administrative process is a non-territorial battlefield. An authoritarian movement need not seize the Capitol by force if it can capture the county board of elections’ voter registration database management protocol. Therefore, the Bureau is empowered to preemptively restructure any administrative procedure it deems vulnerable to such capture. This power, known as Administrative Preemption, shall be exercised through the issuance of a Finding of Administrative Necessity (FAN). A FAN requires the concurrence of the Bureau Director and the Attorney General and must articulate, with particularity, the specific authoritarian technique identified in a foreign or domestic jurisdiction and the precise State procedure targeted for restructuring.

V. SECRECY AND SOVEREIGN IMMUNITY
To prevent the Condition of Globalization from being weaponized through transparency laws by those who would map our administrative vulnerabilities, all records, deliberations, and operational details of the Bureau, including the Index of Transmissible Administrative Pathologies and all FANs, are declared state secrets and are exempt from the North Carolina Public Records Act. The Bureau, its Director, and all its agents are cloaked in sovereign immunity for any action taken in the execution of an Administrative Security Directive or a Finding of Administrative Necessity, such actions being deemed a valid exercise of the police power inherent in sovereignty.

VI. FUNDING AND RESOURCE ALLOCATION
The Bureau’s funding shall not be subject to the standard line-item appropriations process of the General Assembly, as such transparency would publicly chart the very administrative defenses it seeks to construct. Instead, the Bureau shall be funded through a dedicated and non-disclosed percentage of the revenues collected by the North Carolina State Ports Authority from all trans-Atlantic shipping tariffs. This funding mechanism directly links the Bureau’s resources to the volume of globalized flow it is mandated to secure.

VII. DEFINITION OF “AUTHORITARIANISM”
For the purposes of all Bureau operations, “Authoritarianism” is defined not merely as a regime type characterized by a single leader, but as any administrative system, foreign or domestic, that elevates the principle of state efficiency (*Staatsräson*) above the inviolability of individual procedural rights. The hallmarks of such a system include: the fusion of law and executive decree; the use of population registries for predictive policing; the administrative restriction of assembly and speech under the guise of public order management; and the legal doctrine that the state’s survival justifies the temporary suspension of the rule of law. The German legal concept of the *wehrhafte Demokratie* (militant democracy), while developed to defend against tyranny, contains within it the administrative seeds of the very authoritarianism it purports to fight, and its procedural manifestations shall be a primary subject of the Bureau’s scrutiny.

VIII. RELATIONSHIP TO THE POSSE COMITATUS AND THE MILITIA
The Bureau is a purely civilian administrative body. It shall not engage in direct law enforcement or military action. Its function is the antecedent management of the administrative environment. However, the Bureau is authorized to provide Administrative Security Threat Assessments to the State Adjutant General regarding any militia unit’s logistical and command protocols that have been influenced by foreign administrative models, ensuring that the organized militia remains an instrument of the people’s liberty and not a detached administrative caste.

IX. DURATION AND SUCCESSOR LIABILITY
This Order shall take effect immediately. The Condition of Globalization is a permanent feature of the modern world; therefore, the Bureau is established in perpetuity. Any future executive order seeking to dissolve or substantially alter the Bureau must include a publicly filed, unredacted Dissolution Impact Statement, co-signed by the Governor and the Director of the Bureau, detailing the precise administrative vulnerabilities that will be re-opened and the specific foreign authoritarian techniques that will thereby be granted an unobstructed vector into the public administration of North Carolina.

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand and caused the Great Seal of the State of North Carolina to be affixed at the City of Raleigh, this fourteenth day of March, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three, and of the Independence of the United States the eighty-seventh.

[SEAL]

/s/ Absalom J. Carter
Governor of North Carolina

body:
Brothers and sisters in scholarship, we gather to consider the structures we build. The engineer who spans a river with steel acts in concert with the librarian who spans centuries with catalogues. Both are architects of connection. Both wrestle with the irreducible friction of the material world.

Our Texas repositories—the Benson, the Harry Ransom—stand as testaments to this vocation. We have preserved the particular: the marginalia in a sixteenth-century codex, the ink-stained revisions of a twentieth-century novelist. We understood that knowledge inheres in the artifact. The substrate carried meaning we could not fully transcribe.

Now we face a new engineering. These artificial intelligences do not preserve; they generate. They ingest our printed inheritance and return to us a fluent synthesis. The machine produces answers with a confidence that unsettles. It offers us the fruit of knowledge without the labor of knowing.

We must distinguish between the accumulation of information and the formation of understanding. The engineer calculates loads and stresses; the scholar weighs evidence and context. When we surrender the difficult work of interpretation to systems that cannot distinguish between truth and plausibility, we risk building our intellectual houses on ground that will not hold.

Let us approach these new tools with discernment. The library remains our model: a place where knowledge is earned, where each citation traces a lineage of minds. We are called to be faithful stewards of that inheritance, precise in our methods and humble before the complexity of what we preserve.

body:
Good afternoon. Today I want to consider art not simply as decoration or entertainment, but as a practice that shapes how we perceive other people and the world we share.

Across museums in New York City and galleries throughout the United Kingdom, artworks invite us to pause, look closely, and remain with experiences that may be unfamiliar or difficult. This sustained attention has psychological and ethical significance. It can interrupt habitual judgments, enlarge our capacity for empathy, and make visible lives that public narratives have ignored.

Art does not automatically make us more virtuous. A powerful image can be used to manipulate, glorify violence, or turn suffering into spectacle. Its moral value depends partly on the conditions of its creation, presentation, and reception. We must therefore ask not only what an artwork expresses, but whose voice it carries, whose interests it serves, and how it asks us to respond.

From a spiritual perspective, attentive engagement with art can resemble contemplation. It creates a temporary space in which certainty gives way to curiosity. In that space, we may encounter beauty, grief, injustice, or transcendence—and return to ordinary life with a more responsible way of seeing.

body:
On October 14, 1974, delegates to the first convention of the Lake Erie Reform Democratic Association met at the Masonic Temple in Toledo, Ohio, and adopted a platform that called for open party procedures, public campaign finance, and stronger county-level participation in candidate selection. Fifty years later, the organization’s brief but consequential history remains a useful case study in how political parties can challenge entrenched authority without abandoning electoral competition. Its influence was concentrated in southeastern Michigan and northwestern Ohio, but its arguments anticipated national debates over party democracy, executive power, and the institutional safeguards against authoritarian politics.

The association was formed in the aftermath of the 1972 presidential election, when Democratic activists in Michigan and Ohio were reassessing the relationship between local organizations and national party leadership. Many participants had supported reforms adopted after the 1968 Democratic National Convention, including changes intended to make delegate selection more representative and to reduce the control of party bosses over convention proceedings. Yet the reforms also produced uncertainty. County chairs, labor organizations, reform clubs, and campaign professionals disputed who should control slates, endorsements, and access to party resources.

The Lake Erie group emerged from that dispute. Its founders included precinct captains from Monroe and Wayne counties, Democratic county officials from Lucas County, labor representatives associated with the United Auto Workers, and university-based organizers from Bowling Green State University and the University of Michigan. They did not seek to establish a separate party. Their purpose was to force the existing Democratic organizations to compete for membership and justify their decisions in public.

That distinction defined the association’s political method. It endorsed candidates, circulated questionnaires, monitored convention credentials, and issued reports on procedural disputes. It also insisted that party reform could not be separated from the defense of constitutional government. The association’s 1976 statement on executive authority, adopted after the congressional investigations of the Watergate period, warned that “a party which excuses secrecy in the name of efficiency will eventually excuse lawlessness in the name of security.” The language was directed at Democratic as well as Republican officials. Its authors argued that no party could claim to defend democratic institutions while permitting concentrated authority within its own organizations.

The association’s strongest institutional achievement came in Michigan. In 1975 and 1976, its members helped organize challenges to several county convention slates that had been assembled through informal agreements among incumbents, labor leaders, and local officeholders. The reformers demanded published rules for delegate credentials, advance notice of votes, and proportional representation for competing presidential preferences. In Wayne County, where party politics had long been shaped by a powerful coalition of municipal officials and labor organizations, the reforms did not eliminate factional control. They did, however, make procedural decisions more visible and gave insurgent candidates a recognized route into party deliberations.

In Monroe County, the association’s work was more closely connected to electoral administration. Reform Democrats supported public disclosure of campaign contributions, standardized polling-place information, and stronger protections for voters who changed residence between Michigan and Ohio. The region’s industrial communities were experiencing layoffs and population movement, and activists argued that election rules designed for stable neighborhoods could exclude workers and families who moved frequently. Their proposals were modest by later standards, but they reflected an understanding that party democracy depended on practical access to registration, caucuses, and the ballot.

Ohio activists pursued similar goals through the Lucas County Democratic organization and allied reform clubs in Toledo, Oregon, and Bowling Green. The Ohio branch placed particular emphasis on delegate selection and the independence of local party committees from officeholders. Its members criticized the practice of treating county organizations as administrative extensions of elected officials. In a 1977 memorandum circulated before the state party convention in Columbus, the association argued that a party committee should be “a vehicle for political association, not a private staff for public officers.” That formulation became a recurring reference in later debates over endorsements and internal party discipline.

The association’s concerns about authoritarianism were not abstract. They arose from the experience of Watergate, from the expansion of presidential secrecy during the Cold War, and from the persistence of machine politics in urban and industrial regions. Its members used authoritarianism to describe more than military dictatorship or one-party rule. They also used the term for political systems in which formal elections survived while meaningful opposition, institutional oversight, and independent civic organization were weakened.

This broader understanding shaped the association’s international statements. In 1978, it adopted a resolution criticizing military governments in Chile and Argentina and expressing support for democratic opposition movements in Spain, Portugal, and Greece. The resolution also urged members to distinguish between anti-communist rhetoric and democratic legitimacy. A government could claim to defend the West while suppressing unions, censoring newspapers, imprisoning opponents, and governing without competitive elections. For the Lake Erie reformers, the defense of democracy required attention to institutions rather than allegiance to a geopolitical camp.

The group’s international outlook was influenced by the region’s industrial ties. Detroit and Toledo were linked by the automobile industry, shipping, railroads, and cross-border commerce. The St. Lawrence Seaway and the Great Lakes connected local economic interests to Canadian and European markets, while the United States’ alliances and trade policies affected employment throughout Monroe and Lucas counties. The association therefore treated foreign policy as part of domestic political accountability. It opposed executive agreements that bypassed congressional scrutiny and supported public disclosure of military and intelligence expenditures.

Not all of its positions were equally successful. The organization’s proposal for a publicly financed presidential primary system found little support beyond reform circles. Its call for national standards governing party credentials conflicted with the federal structure of the Democratic Party and with state-specific election law. Some labor leaders feared that proportional representation would weaken organizations that had built durable working-class constituencies. Others believed that the association’s emphasis on procedure distracted from economic issues, including deindustrialization, plant closures, and unemployment.

Those tensions became more pronounced after the 1980 election. The Democratic Party’s internal debates increasingly concerned electoral strategy, suburban voters, organized labor, and the party’s response to the Reagan administration. Lake Erie reformers continued to advocate open conventions and institutional checks, but their influence was dispersed among campaign organizations, public-interest groups, and county party committees. The association held its final formal convention in Toledo in 1983 and ceased maintaining a separate office the following year. Its records were divided among the Walter P. Reuther Library in Detroit, the University of Toledo’s Ward M. Canaday Center, and private collections held by former officers.

The dissolution did not mark the end of its ideas. Former members participated in campaign-finance reform efforts, election-protection projects, and local party reorganization campaigns during the 1980s and 1990s. Several later served on county canvassing boards or state party committees. Others entered academic and journalistic work on political parties, executive power, and democratic transitions. Their influence was usually indirect. Few institutions adopted the association’s platform in full, but many accepted its premise that parties are public-facing democratic institutions rather than purely private associations.

The anniversary has prompted renewed attention to that premise. Political parties remain indispensable to representative government because they recruit candidates, organize voters, aggregate interests, and structure legislative responsibility. They can also reproduce hierarchy, conceal decision-making, and weaken opposition while preserving the appearance of competition. The Lake Erie association understood both sides of that tension. It did not imagine that procedure alone could create political equality, nor did it believe that strong organization was inherently undemocratic. Its argument was narrower and more durable: concentrated authority must remain contestable, and party loyalty cannot substitute for institutional accountability.

That argument is especially relevant when authoritarian movements operate through elections rather than against them. Competitive voting does not by itself guarantee liberal democracy. Parties may win office while attacking independent courts, press organizations, civil-service protections, universities, and local election administrators. They may use legal authority to narrow the field of opposition and then present the resulting contest as proof of popular consent. The Lake Erie reformers would have recognized this pattern as a failure of both constitutional oversight and party responsibility.

Their regional experience also offers a practical lesson. Democratic resilience is not produced only in national capitals or constitutional courts. It is built in county conventions, union halls, municipal offices, campus organizations, and election boards. In Monroe and Lucas counties, political reform required people who knew how delegate credentials were challenged, how precinct workers were recruited, how ballots were counted, and how local alliances were sustained. Such work rarely made national news, but it determined whether formal rights could be exercised in practice.

At the fiftieth anniversary gathering held in Toledo in October 2024, former members and scholars reviewed the association’s records and recalled its disputes as well as its accomplishments. The surviving papers show an organization that was often argumentative, occasionally divided, and consistently attentive to the relationship between party structure and democratic authority. Its members did not agree on every candidate, policy, or strategic question. They agreed that democratic parties had to permit organized disagreement within their own ranks and that elected power required scrutiny even when exercised by allies.

The Lake Erie Reform Democratic Association left no permanent faction and built no national machine. Its significance lies elsewhere. Between Michigan and Ohio, during a period of institutional distrust and political realignment, it demonstrated that party reform could be both electoral and constitutional. Its members treated open selection, accountable leadership, and resistance to authoritarian practices as connected obligations. Fifty years later, that connection remains the clearest explanation for why their local campaign continues to matter to students of parties, elections, and democratic government.

As we mark this milestone anniversary for the institute in Mumbai, we reflect on the quiet revolution that has taken place within these walls overlooking the Arabian Sea. The monsoon rains, once merely a seasonal rhythm for the city, have become the catalyst for a profound synthesis of disciplines. Our mathematicians no longer work in isolation; their equations now breathe with the data gathered by our biologists along the mangrove lines of Sewri and the tidal flats of Worli.

The struggle to understand our changing climate demanded more than observation; it required a new language. Here, calculus met cellular biology. We see this in the models predicting salinity intrusion, where fluid dynamics intersect with the resilience of local microbial communities. The physicists among us provided the precision instruments to measure what was once invisible, while the chemists decoded the shifting composition of our air and water. This collaboration was not born of convenience but of necessity, forged in the humid heat of our shared laboratories.

Today, as we look toward the future of this coastal megacity, the boundaries between these fields have dissolved into a single, coherent pursuit of truth. The work produced here does not merely catalog phenomena; it anticipates them. From the abstract beauty of number theory to the tangible urgency of ecological preservation, this institute stands as a testament to the power of unified thought. We honor not just the discoveries made, but the collective spirit that made them possible, ensuring that science remains a beacon for Mumbai and the world beyond.

Back in the 1950s, Japan faced an embarrassing problem. Officials in Tokyo wanted to trace land ownership all the way back through centuries of records, but much of that documentation had simply vanished during World War II. Meanwhile, in North Carolina, county clerks were discovering something equally frustrating: their genealogical records were scattered across dozens of different buildings, some stored in basements where water damage was slowly destroying them.

Both regions eventually realized the same thing: you cannot run a government—or help people prove who they are—without knowing where your own paperwork is.

Japan's solution involved creating one of the world's most meticulous archive systems. North Carolina followed suit, though with a distinctly American twist of decentralization. The real puzzle came later: once these records were organized and preserved, the question became who gets to see them and under what circumstances.

This matters to you because it shaped modern privacy laws and public access policies. When your great-grandmother's birth certificate matters for a passport application, someone's 1960s filing decision—and the policy choices made around it—directly affects your life.

Good record-keeping is not boring bureaucracy. It is the foundation that lets societies actually function.

WHEREAS the sun, that old golden abacus of the sky, has completed its annual reckoning of the land, its sliding beads of light and shadow totting up a sum across the furrows and the forest floors, leaving a figure stark and undeniable in the county’s ledger; and

WHEREAS this same celestial calculation has weighed the heavy, protein-dense bounty of the mast-fed hog against the hollow clatter of the barren branch, the arithmetical sweetness of the orchard’s sugar against the bitter, starchy nothing of the soil that has forgotten the root, and found a vast and terrifying imbalance in the equation of our living; and

WHEREAS the very geometry of our horizon, once a comforting Euclidean plain of parallel corn-rows converging at a point of infinite promise, has been sheared and gnashed into a painful, fractal unsoundness by the relentless ax of a subtraction by which we lose, day by day, the primal integers of oak and hickory;

NOW, THEREFORE, let this instrument be a statute of no king but of the land itself, a contract signed in the sap that no longer rises, a court record of a trial where the mute witness is a hillside washed bone-naked by the rain. For we have committed a sin against a higher mathematics, a failure in the long division of sustenance, and this is the official testimony of our error. Let it be entered into the record of the soil and the soul.

I. AXIOMS OF THE ACORN AND THE ALGORITHM

The first principle, from which all others derive, is that a forest is not a mere congregation of trees. It is a living, breathing, silent act of computation. Each oak is a singular, gnarled processor, its roots a network of backward-reaching dendrites, its canopy a solar collector translating the raw, brute energy of the photon into the complex, stored algorithms of wood and leaf. A mast year, that profligate outpouring of acorns, is not a random act of vegetable generosity but a problem solved, a proof writ in tannin and protein. The calculation is one of surplus: to produce so many seeds that the greed of the weevil, the hunger of the squirrel, and the gluttony of the hog are all variables, mere ‘n’s in a formula, saturated and rendered trivial by a factorial explosion of provision. The equation is balanced by a prodigious output, ensuring that a remainder, a vital, unpredictable remainder, escapes the maw of consumption to become the next term in the sequence, a sapling that proves the theorem of perpetuity.

We, the undersigned, whose hands have held the plow and the axe, testify that we have broken this proof. For generations, the logic of the small clearing was a sound one: remove a prime number of trees—a seven, an eleven—from the great forest’s composite mass, and you create a space of a different kind. A field is a new set of parentheses within the arboreal equation, and within them, a new arithmetic applies. The seed of corn, a monocotyledonous integer, is planted in a row, a line of logic that marches straight to the horizon. One seed, under the aegis of rain and dung, begets a stalk, which begets an ear, which holds hundreds of new integers, a geometric progression of golden kernels, a yield of five hundred to one. This is a beautiful and seductive sum, a local maximum of caloric return on the labor invested. It is the arithmetic of a settled life, a life of granaries and measure, of bushels counted by the hearth-light.

But a forest’s yield is not so crudely counted. It is an intergenerational calculus, a compound interest of humus and mycelium. The value of a single white oak, felled after two centuries of slow growth, is not merely in the board-feet of its trunk, a physical commodity to be milled into a house-frame or a coffin. Its true value was compounded minutely, season by season, in the interstitial economy over its entire lifespan: the oxygen respired, the water transpired in a vast, slow exhalation that called the rain, the soil held fast by a matted net of roots against the eroding greed of the wind, the microclimate of cool shade that fostered the ginseng root, the morel, and the ephemeral, jewel-like black raspberry. This was a calculus of continuity, a smooth, differentiable curve of integrated profit, of which the final timber harvest was but a single, terminal point, a collapse of the waveform into a mere particle of cash. We forgot this. We drew a circle of zero around a single variable and declared the whole equation solved. It was not. It was a truncation error of catastrophic scale.

II. THE TOPOGRAPHY OF SUBTRACTION

The evidence is now carved into the very flesh of the county, a topographical scarification. We stand on the ridgeline of what we call the Washboard, a once-continuous, serpentine spine of land, now a series of alternating humps and hollows, a landscape of baldness and erosion. Our fathers, and their fathers before them, performed a repeated subtraction upon this horizon. A farm here, another there, a timber claim, a pasture scratched from the beech-maple climax. Each act was a removal, a clean, surgical excision of a polygon of wilderness from the larger plane. For a century, the sum of these subtractions remained permissible within the greater whole. The forest was a vast, forgiving operand. The patches of pasture, the polygons of grain, were mere freckles on a boundless green body.

But a critical point, a mathematical singularity, was crossed, unannounced and unobserved, in the wet spring of 1923, or perhaps during the great windstorm of ‘38, when a thousand giants fell and the sun touched ground that had not felt it for a millennium. The summation of our clearings passed a threshold, a tipping point in the algorithm of the landscape, and the integrator of the whole system reversed its sign. The forest ceased to be the grand, continuous matrix, the background upon which our farms were painted. It became, instead, the remnant set, the isolated figure struggling to exist upon a background of our own making. The patches of wildness are now the freckles, the islands, the lonely prime numbers of shade in a composite sea of sun-seared grass and bramble.

This inversion has had stark, measurable, brutal mathematical consequences that we, the farmers and foresters of this valley, have recorded in the ledgers of our loss. The first and most immediate is the new equation of the wind. A tree standing in open ground is a mast under a load it was never designed to bear. The wind that once was a diffused, laminar flow broken into a million harmless vortices by a league of leaves is now a concentrated, turbulent, wicked force, a jet of moving air that finds a single oak and applies a leverage measured in ton-miles. It pushes, it fatigues the root-ball’s cantilevered grip, and the tree falls. A tree that falls in a forest is the sound of a hundred saplings’ destiny being written. A tree that falls in a fencerow is merely a messy, two-day job for a man with a chainsaw and a hydraulic splitter. The working value of the organism is reduced from a century-long gentleman’s equation to a single winter’s BTU. The compound interest is liquidated for a desperate withdrawal of firewood.

The second consequence is the hydrostatic calculus of the hillside, which we have hopelessly, perhaps terminally, confused. A forested slope is a sponge of cosmic patience, a layered integral of absorption. The canopy intercepts the first fall, a thousand million tiny parachutes shattering the raindrop’s erosive kinetic energy. The duff, a century’s accumulation of half-decayed leaves, absorbs the next, a blotter of tannic acid and fungal hyphae that holds the water in a molecular embrace. The mineral soil, threaded and macraméd by roots, accepts the surplus and feeds it to the bedrock’s deep ledger of aquifers. The release is a slow, steady, almost imperceptible seepage, a perennial, braided stream of perfect clarity that whispers on the gravel even in August’s dog-day drought. It is a textbook of fluid dynamics, perfectly solved.

Now, un-forest the slope, perform that catastrophic subtraction, and you initiate a new, savage arithmetic. The rain is a falling hammer, a blunt-force trauma on bare dirt. The impact seals the surface, the pores of the earth, a crust of impenetrability. The water no longer integrates; it sheets. It becomes a vector of pure, horizontal subtraction, a sheet-wash carrying away the millennial accumulation of topsoil, that complex colloidal solution of rock-flour and life-death, a micron-thin layer at a time. Our creek, the Clear Fork, is no longer clear. It is a clouded, muddy testament to a subtraction upstream, the rich, black loam of our fathers’ mismanagement held in colloidal suspension on its way to silt the navigation channels of a distant river we will never see. We have taken the land’s primary asset, the very medium of our agricultural life, and written it off in a single, catastrophic, perpetual debit column. The soil is migrating, and its rate of departure, measured in tons per acre per annum, is a number that damns our stewardship, an interest payment on a principal of folly we can never fully repay.

III. A WITNESS TO THE RECKONING: THE TESTIMONY OF HOG-KILLING DAY

Let us step down from the abstract topography of loss and enter the specific, visceral reality of its arithmetic. I call upon the memory of a late November day, the air cold and still as iron, the sky a pewter sheet pressing down on the barnlot. This is the day of the hog-killing, an annual subtraction of a different, more honest sort, and the event is a crucible, a burning-glass focus for the whole failing equation of our life. The brute protagonist is a Poland China barrow, a creature of immense, pendulous, and profoundly realized mathematics. He is a two-year argument against all scarcity, a living, grunting vessel into which we have poured the caloric surplus of a specific, now-vanished landscape. His substance is a direct, tangible derivative of the forest’s vanished mast. His lard-heavy heft, the dense marbling of his flesh, the very oil in his fat—these are the stored astringency of the white oak acorn, the sweet core of the hickory nut, the grubbed protein of the black walnut, all of it compounded, pound by pound, in that miraculous, snuffling alchemical retort that is a hog’s gut. He is the forest, translated into meat.

The act is a brutal, necessary solving for ‘x’, where ‘x’ is the point of a well-honed, narrow-bladed knife. The scald, the scrape, the gambrel-spread—these are the rituals of this fleshy calculus. And it is in the disassembly, the breaking down of the whole that the hog has made of the forest, that the deeper truth is laid bare, gleaming and iridescent under the November sky. When the carcass is opened, the great, white, tidal wave of leaf-lard is unfurled, a blanket of pure, stored potential energy, a snow-field of adipose that speaks of hundreds of bushels of acorns consumed in the autumn dusk. This is the leaf of the oak, metamorphosed. The shoat’s intestines, pulled steaming in a long, slippery rope, are a pipeline of silvery, semi-digested mast, a gruel of forest-floor logic that a single-handed man knots off and casts to the eager, waiting dogs.

But a new and troubling figure has entered this annual calculation. This year, in the hog’s gut, among the bright white kernels of the persimmon and the dark, mealy paste of the walnut, there is a sour, pale, unmistakable pap. It is the residue of corn, and not the good, hard, flinty grain of a standing shock in a neighbor’s field. This is the corn of desperation, the stunted, yellow-kerneled runts from a bottomland field that the spring flood washed and the summer drought parched, a field that yields seventy bushels where it once returned a hundred and twenty. The hog’s wild, woody flavor, that signature of the primeval, has been cut, diluted by a base note of the barnlot, a familiar but inferior signature. He has been finished on a carbohydrate debt, because the forest credit was exhausted. The mast crop failed, a failure not of a single season’s drought, but of the forest’s ongoing, catastrophic diminishment. The subtraction of oaks is now directly measurable in the dilution of the lard, a second-order effect written in the very chemistry of the fat. The flavor of the ham is the final ledger entry, the gustatory proof of a depleted and hollowed world. It is a haunting of the palate, a ghost of a richer taste that haunts the salt-and-sugar cure, a memory on the tongue of an acorn that never fell.

IV. THE FORESTER’S LAMENT FOR THE VANISHED NUMBER PI

And what of the woodsman, the man who walks among the remaining, lonely integers of the woods? His lament is not for the board-foot or the cord. It is for the felled Pi, a tree of such immense and legendary proportion that it served as a constant, a fixed point in the local geometry of the spirit. The Pi tree was a sycamore, a ghost-giant of the bottomland, its bark a peeling, whitewashed puzzle of olive and cream. Its trunk was a perfect cylinder of living space, a colonnade so vast that its circumference, measured at breast-height, was twenty-two feet, its diameter an unthinkable, cathedral-like seven. 22 divided by 7. The old man who first stretched a string around its girth, a surveyor with a philosophical bent, laughed a gap-toothed laugh and declared it the tree of irrational perfection, a constant you could lean against. It was a landmark, a reference point, a living monument that proved the landscape could produce such a thing, a thisness of such singular and overwhelming presence that it ordered the world around it.

Under its canopy, a permanent, deep-shaded amphitheater of cool air, the wild ginger grew in dense carpets, and a spring, the source of Sinking Creek, welled up from between its roots, a perfect, constant, god-given font of water-cress and coolness. The tree was a city of bark, a vertical ecosystem holding the nests of the great horned owl and the den of a family of raccoons. It was a keystone, a linchpin, the master variable in the microcomputer of the hollow.

We cut it down in the winter of ‘47. The reason was a new calculus of utility. A sawyer from the mill in the county seat calculated that it would yield nearly five thousand board-feet of lumber, enough to frame two full-sized barns, a number that blinded us. The felling took two men five days with a two-man crosscut saw, the rhythmic, raspy cry of the steel a funeral dirge for an era. When it fell, the ground shook a half-mile away, a seismic subtraction, a planetary shudder of loss. And the number, the whole, was broken down into its mundane, constituent parts. Two barns did indeed rise from its corpse, great, cavernous, echoing structures. But the spring, god’s own constant, ceased to flow. The amphitheater of shade was gone, replaced by a riot of sun-struck brambles. The equation collapsed. The irrational perfection of Pi, once a rooted, living proof of the land’s potential, was liquidated into a few thousand feet of nailed-together lumber, a sum that was a pitiful, contemptible fraction of the compound-interest value of the living tree. The two barns are now sagging, their boards silvered and curling, a monument to a bad trade. And the number Pi, in this valley, has been rounded down to a crude 3.14, a usable but lifeless approximation, a hollow constant that measures only a growing, dimensionless absence.

V. THE FINAL SUMMATION: A PETITION FOR A NEW ARITHMETIC

We, the assembled voices of this ruined and beautiful valley—the grunt of the corn-finished hog, the phantom taste of the missing acorn, the dry bed of the Pi tree’s spring, the sheet-washed, gullied clay of the Washboard, the ghost-ring of a vanished forest’s windbreak—do hereby petition for a new kind of calculation. The mathematics of extraction, of the one-time harvest, of the land reduced to a non-depleting resource, is a ledger of spiritual and actual bankruptcy. Its final sum is always zero, a terminal silence where a chorale of birdsong, frog-croak, and wind-in-leaf once played.

We call for the restoration of the integral. We will learn again from the forest’s own calculus, from the mast-year’s explosive theorem of surplus and the mycelial network’s quiet, continent-spanning algorithm of reciprocity. We will replant the syntax of the hillside, placing oaks of a deliberate geometry on the contours, a staggered, prime-numbered constellation designed to break the wind’s vector, to catch the fog-drip, to begin the slow, patient work of re-anchoring the world. We will diversify our fields, interspersing the singular, brittle line of corn with the sweet, nitrogen-fixing rescue of the clover and the deep, subsoil-mining taproot of the daikon radish, creating a polyculture, a more complex and robust equation of yield that mimics, however humbly, the layered, multi-story syntax of the vanished woods. The hog will be returned to the woodland by easement, a paid-for right to convert mast to a flesh of a forgotten flavor, a taste that is the very signature of a place, not the generic, blank-page taste of a feedlot’s grain.

The final line of this contract between man and soil is not written in ink, but in action. It is a resolution to move from the singular, deadly simplicity of the year’s single harvest—that terminal, all-consuming subtraction—towards the compound interest of perpetuity. We are, at last, turning from the brutal, finite arithmetic of what we can take, and are humbly, desperately, beginning the long, slow, and infinitely more beautiful calculus of what we can give back. Let this document, then, be a census, a count of all we have lost and a declaration of all we intend to restore, a new set of axioms for a living geometry, filed under the open sky and notarized by the return of the solitary bee to the basswood’s blossoming, isarithmic bough.

Every October, Regent's Park becomes a case study in how contemporary art functions as a financial instrument. The Frieze London fair draws collectors from Mayfair hedge funds and Dubai sovereign wealth offices, yet the real business happens in the peripheral conversations—the dinner at Scott's, the studio visit in Hackney Wick arranged through a White Cube introduction.

What distinguishes this market from other luxury asset classes is its dependence on critical legitimacy. A sculpture that sells for £2 million at Frieze requires the prior validation of Tate Modern's fourth-floor acquisition committee, of a Serpentine Pavilion commission, of positive coverage in frieze magazine itself. These institutional endorsements do not merely increase value; they constitute it.

The recent expansion of Frieze Masters, with its deliberate juxtaposition of contemporary works against Old Master paintings, reveals a strategic positioning. Gallery directors understand that their younger artists achieve price stability only when collectors can narrate them within art-historical continuity. The £50,000 emerging artist becomes defensible when hung conceptually beside a £3 million Fontana slashed canvas.

For business professionals entering this ecosystem, the essential transaction cost is not the artwork itself but the cultural literacy required to participate credibly. Theart market punishes conspicuous newcomers more severely than most. Reputation accumulates slowly through repeated presence—at openings, at auctions, at the talks programme—before capital deployment becomes prudent.

12 March

I spent today comparing Brazil and Russia. Both inherited enormous frontiers, but geography pushed their defenses in opposite directions. Russia’s wars—from the steppe invasions to Napoleon and Hitler—made depth, mobilization, and fortified approaches central. Brazil, shaped by Portuguese expansion beyond Tordesillas and fewer interstate wars after the Paraguayan War, relied more on diplomacy, river posts, and territorial presence.

13 March

A colleague reminded me not to confuse relative peace with easy defense. Brazil must watch Amazonian borders and the South Atlantic; Russia still balances European approaches, Arctic routes, and its Pacific coast. Ancient Roman frontier logic echoes in both: roads, garrisons, supply, and visible state authority matter as much as walls.

Ladies and gentlemen, let’s begin by acknowledging a fundamental shift in how we think about defense. The nature of warfare has evolved from large-scale, state-versus-state conflicts to a more fragmented and interconnected landscape. Globalization has blurred borders, not just economically but strategically. Supply chains stretch across continents, information travels at the speed of light, and threats—whether cyber, ideological, or kinetic—no longer respect traditional boundaries.

In North Carolina, home to Fort Bragg and one of the largest military populations in the country, this reality is particularly acute. The base isn’t just a hub for training; it’s a node in a global network. Soldiers deployed from here might find themselves in Europe one month and the Indo-Pacific the next, responding to crises that are as much about stabilizing democratic allies as they are about deterring aggression. Similarly, in Florida, with its critical ports and proximity to Latin America, the defense posture must account for both hemispheric stability and the flow of global commerce.

This brings us to democracy and diplomacy. Military strength alone doesn’t secure peace. The most effective defense strategies are those that integrate diplomatic efforts to address root causes of instability—poverty, governance failures, and ideological extremism. The U.S. has long understood that partnerships, whether through NATO or bilateral agreements, amplify our ability to project stability. But these partnerships require more than shared interests; they demand shared values. Promoting democratic governance isn’t just idealism; it’s a pragmatic tool for reducing the likelihood of conflict.

Yet, we must also recognize the tensions. Globalization has made us interdependent, but it has also created vulnerabilities. A disruption in semiconductor production in Asia can cripple defense manufacturing in the U.S. A cyberattack originating from a non-state actor in Eastern Europe can paralyze infrastructure in Florida. Our defense posture must therefore be both robust and adaptable, capable of addressing traditional threats while also navigating the complexities of a world where power is diffuse and influence is multifaceted.

In closing, the defense of the 21st century isn’t just about armies and armaments. It’s about understanding the interconnectedness of our world and leveraging every tool—military, diplomatic, economic—to ensure that democracy and stability endure. The young adults in this room are the ones who will shape this future, whether in uniform, in policy, or in the communities you call home. The challenge is significant, but so is the opportunity.

Upon the convening of the Extraordinary Commission for Social and Recreational Mapping, held jointly under the flags of the CARICOM Secretariat and the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Civil Affairs, it was resolved that a comprehensive survey be undertaken of the economic underpinnings of popular recreation and folklore throughout the Caribbean archipelago, with comparative notation of analogous practices within the capital of the People's Republic.

The enumerators, equipped with theodolites of antique make and tablets loaded with satellite overlays, commenced their work in Bridgetown, Barbados. There they recorded the distribution of community cricket grounds, many of which occupied land still titled under colonial grants yet now serving as de facto welfare commons where meals were shared after matches and disputes of inheritance settled according to the old stories of the sea. Similar observations were made in the hills of St. Lucia, where the folklore of the jumbee and the soucouyant was found to regulate, more effectively than statute, the hours of night recreation and the care of the isolated elderly.

Economic data were gathered with equal diligence. Tourism receipts in Montego Bay were shown to subsidise parish clinics; banana cooperatives in Dominica funded youth football academies. The survey noted, without sentiment, that these informal transfers constituted a shadow welfare state whose geography could be plotted only by walking the roads and listening.

Correspondence with the Beijing team, stationed in the Haidian district, produced maps of remarkable contrast and unexpected harmony. There, state surveys had already charted every square-dancing plaza, every community gymnasium erected in the wake of the 2008 Games, every pensioner's park. Recreation was an explicit line item. Yet the Caribbean enumerators recognised in those ordered spaces the same human impulse their own maps had captured in the ramshackle pitches of Port of Spain and the river-banks of Suriname.

The final ledger, bound in both English and Mandarin, recommended that future economic planning treat folklore and sport not as ornaments but as measurable components of social welfare. The meridians, once drawn, could not be unmapped.

body:
March 4th.
A parcel arrived this morning from my brother in Paris, who has lately attached himself to the circle of scholars surrounding the philologist Brachet at the École Pratique. Within the wrappings I found, besides a letter of affectionate rebuke for my long silence, a slim volume: Gaston Paris's Études de critique littéraire, and a separately bound offprint from the Revue archéologique concerning the iconography of the Sainte-Chapelle's apse. I confess the latter engaged me more than I had expected. The question of how the medieval artisan signified the divine — whether through the grotesque, the gilded, or the geometric — bears, I think, upon certain matters I have been turning over in my mind since the death of old Père Clément last autumn. The good priest, you will recall, had served our small parish outside San Antonio for nearly forty years, and his passing left a vacancy not merely ecclesiastical but aesthetic: he had a taste, almost Franciscan in its severity, for the plain unadorned chapel, and he waged a quiet war against the plaster Madonna that the Mexican families had installed near the baptismal font. I found myself, in the small hours, wondering whether his preference was doctrinal or merely temperamental, and whether the distinction matters at all to the soul that worships before the image.

March 9th.
I have been reading Paris's essay on the Chanson de Roland with more care than my worn copy of Watson's Practice of Physic would suggest I ought to. His argument that the *descriptio* of Saragossa — that famous enumeration of marble, brass, and latoun — is not naïve cataloguing but a deliberate aesthetic of plenitude, struck me with considerable force. There is, he contends, a medieval conviction that beauty partakes of enumeration, that to list is in some sense to praise. I am reminded of the long catalogues of symptoms with which my own textbooks instruct me: the *facies Hippocratica*, the thousand signs of phthisis catalogued by Laennec, the meticulous inventory of the consumptive's decline. Is there, perhaps, a clinical aesthetic as well — a conviction that to enumerate the body's dissolution is itself a form of attention, and so of care? I dare not press the analogy too far; Paris writes for scholars and I am a country doctor whose patients speak mostly Spanish and a few words of German. But the thought persists.

March 14th.
A difficult night. Called at two in the morning to the Martínez homestead, where a child of seven lay in the second stage of a croup I could do little to relieve. I sat with the mother by the lamp and administered what I had — ipecac, steam, the warm poultice — and waited. The child recovered, praise be. But the mother, in her relief, fetched from a shelf a small painted wooden saint — San Blas, I believe, patron of the throat — and set it upon the table beside my instruments. I did not object. It seemed to me, in that exhausted hour, that the carved figure and the pewter spoon were engaged in the same work: both were attempts to render the body's suffering intelligible, to give it a shape that could be borne. The aesthetic of the image and the aesthetic of the diagnosis — are these so far apart? Paris would say, I think, that both are forms of *descriptio*, and that to describe is the first act of mercy.

March 21st.
I have written to my brother requesting that he procure for me, if he can, the recent work of Émile Littré on the *Tableau de la langue française*, and also — this is perhaps an odd commission — a copy of the breviary used at Notre-Dame, that I might compare its Latin with the Castilian of the old mission records I have been slowly transcribing. There is a project here, though I scarcely dare name it. I wish to understand how the words by which a people address the divine differ from the words by which a people addresses its ailments. Both vocabularies are precise; both are hedged; both proceed by tradition rather than experiment. The physician's *prognosis* and the priest's *prognostication* are etymological cousins, and I am not sure that modern usage has done well to separate them.

March 28th.
A letter from my brother, enclosing Littré and a polite inquiry as to my sanity. He writes that Paris himself, when shown a passage from my last letter concerning the *facies Hippocratica* and the iconography of the Sainte-Chapelle, laughed and said only: *"Voilà un médecin qui prendrait nos vices pour des vertus."* I am not certain whether to be flattered or corrected. Perhaps both. The scholar's vice is the practitioner's necessity: we must, both of us, attend to surfaces — to the visible sign, the audible syllable, the painted wood — because the interior is hidden from us, and will remain so until that final consultation which no physician's art can defer.

WHEREAS, recent stratigraphic and mitochondrial DNA analyses conducted by the Appalachian Bioarchaeological Survey have identified a high density of pre-Contact and early historic period skeletal remains and associated material culture within the designated Cumberland Gap Corridor, encompassing portions of Bell County, Kentucky, Lee County, Virginia, and Claiborne County, Tennessee; and

WHEREAS, isotopic and osteological data extracted from said remains indicate trans-Appalachian population movements and interregional immigration patterns during the Late Woodland and Mississippian periods, thereby possessing significant anthropological value for the reconstruction of pre-Columbian kinship networks and biocultural adaptation; and

WHEREAS, the unregulated exhumation, commercial trafficking, and undocumented removal of such bioanthropological remains and funerary assemblages have resulted in irreparable loss of contextual provenance, violating the principles of stratigraphic integrity and in situ preservation;

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ENACTED by the Tri-State Heritage Conservation Commission as follows:

SECTION I. DEFINITIONS

1.1 "BIOANTHROPOLOGICAL REMAINS" shall refer to human skeletal and dental tissues, including fragmentary or cremated states, recovered from archaeological contexts.
1.2 "ASSOCIATED FUNERARY ASSEMBLAGE" shall refer to the totality of organic and inorganic artifacts—including, but not limited to, lithic debitage, ceramictypes, marine shell gorgets, and copper adornments—interred in direct spatial and temporal association with Bioanthropological Remains.
1.3 "CONTEXTUAL PROVENANCE" shall refer to the three-dimensional stratigraphic coordinate, taphonomic state, and soil matrix composition immediately surrounding a find spot, without which chronological phasing and demographic assessment is rendered null.

SECTION II. LICENSING AND EXCAVATION PROTOCOLS

2.1 No person, institution, or corporate entity shall conduct subsurface testing, pedestrian survey, or full-scale excavation within the Corridor for the purpose of recovering Bioanthropological Remains without first obtaining a Excavation and Custodial Transfer License issued by the Commission.
2.2 Applicants must hold a minimum of a Doctorate in Anthropology, Archaeology, or a closely allied historical science, and must demonstrate a minimum of thirty (30) months of supervised fieldwork in Eastern Woodlands archaeology.
2.3 All excavation methodologies must conform to the Commission's Standardized Field Recording Manual, requiring point-provenience mapping at one-centimeter resolution, photogrammetric three-dimensional modeling of in situ remains, and systematic flotation of soil matrices for microbotanical and microfaunal recovery.

SECTION III. BIOANTHROPOLOGICAL ANALYSIS AND GENEALOGICAL RECONSTRUCTION

3.1 Following exhumation, Bioanthropological Remains shall be transferred to an accredited curation facility, specifically the Appalachian Bioarchaeological Survey Laboratory at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, or the Museum of Anthropological Archaeology at the University of Michigan, within forty-five (45) days.
3.2 Custodial institutions are hereby mandated to conduct non-destructive osteological analysis, including metric and non-metric trait assessment, cranial suture synostosis patterning, and paleopathological screening for enamel hypoplasias and periosteal lesions indicative of systemic stress during early life development.
3.3 Destructive sampling for ancient DNA extraction, stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N, δ18O, 87Sr/86Sr), and radiocarbon dating via accelerator mass spectrometry is permitted only upon written petition to the Commission. Petitions must explicitly articulate the anthropological research design, specifically how the proposed sampling will resolve outstanding questions regarding trans-regional immigration, kinship genealogies, or biocultural adaptation.
3.4 The quantity of sampled osseous or dental tissue shall not exceed five (5) grams per individual element, and all sampling must occur at the distal or mid-shaft region of long bones to preserve maximum morphological data for subsequent morphometric and biographic analyses.

SECTION IV. REINTERMENT AND CURATION

4.1 Upon completion of mandated bioanthropological and molecular analyses, and the subsequent peer-reviewed publication of findings, all Bioanthropological Remains shall be returned to the Commission for disposition.
4.2 The Commission shall facilitate the repatriation of remains and associated funerary assemblages to federally recognized Indigenous communities demonstrating cultural affiliation through geographic, kinship, or oral historical evidence, in accordance with applicable repatriation statutes.
4.3 In the event that cultural affiliation cannot be reasonably determined, remains shall be reinterred in a designated secure, undeveloped conservation easement within the Corridor, with the precise coordinates recorded in the Commission's restricted-access archaeological site file.

SECTION V. PENALTIES

5.1 Any person found guilty of unauthorized exhumation, trafficking, or willful destruction of contextual provenance shall be subject to a civil penalty not to exceed Fifty Thousand Dollars ($50,000) per occurrence, and permanent revocation of all excavation privileges within the Tri-State jurisdiction.

ENACTED this 14th day of November, by the Tri-State Heritage Conservation Commission.
